📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jorrybell Agoto, the star of Rafael Manuel’s award-winning debut feature Filipiñana, died November 17 following a battle with lymphoma, her family noted. She was 32.

According to recent reports, epicmedia Productions, the Philippine production tech giant behind Filipiñana, posted on its Instagram account: “We love you, Belle. No more pain.”.

Manuel posted: “The tragedy of this loss cannot be put into words. The world has just lost one of its brightest stars. We have just lost a great friend. But our thoughts and prayers go out especially to Jorrybell’s family who have just lost a loving older sister and a devoted daughter.”.

Filipiñana premiered at this year’s Sundance Film Festival, where it won the Special Jury Award for Creative Vision in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition. It is also the Philippines’ entry for the Best International Feature category of next year’s Oscars. Watch on Deadline.

In a recent development, agoto played the lead role of a quiet but determined resort worker at a high-end golf club in the film, which explores themes of gentrification, class and globalization. She also starred in the original short film, Filipiñana (2020), that the feature was based on. Also directed by Manuel, the short won a Silver Bear Jury Prize at the Berlinale.

Sources indicate that born on September 25, 1994, in Ilocos, Philippines, Agoto started acting in community theater at a young age before graduating with a BA in Theater Arts from Polytechnic University of the Philippines. She also had roles in short films including Cross My Heart and Hope t Die and such features as Jun Robles Lana’s Sisa, which premiered at the 2025 Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival, and Lawrence Fajardo’s Silenced Nights, which premiered at this year’s Toronto Film Festival.

The Film Development Council of the Philippines also issued a statement following the news of her passing: “The Film Development Council of the Philippines extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of Ms. Jorrybell Agoto — Lead Actress, Filipiñana (1994–2026). Your contribution to the Philippine film industry will remain etched in our hearts. Thank you so much, and farewell, Jorrybell.”.

Kino Lorber, which is distributing Filipiñana in the U.S., also remembered the young actress and paid tribute to her talent: “While we never met Jorrybell, we felt like we had through the light she brought to Isabel in Filipiñana. Cinema is poorer for having lost her so young.”.

It has been revealed that filipiñana is being released in the UK and Ireland this weekend by BFI Distribution. Kino Lorber released the film in the U.S. in August and is organizing a series of screenings as part of its Oscar campaign.

In Can’t Hardly Wait, six high school seniors attend their grad night house party, where Preston Meyers (Ethan Embry) intends to give his long time crush Amanda (Hewitt) a love letter after their chance encounter four years before.

‘Much Ado About Nothing’ Broadway Review: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell & Jamie Lloyd Throw An Irresistible Party Of Shakespeare’s Great Comedy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deadline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that outside of ticker tape parades and Newly introduced Year’s Eve in Times Square, you might be hard-pressed to think of a better, more joyous use of floating paper than the confetti that piles up nightly on the stage of Broadway‘s Winter Garden Theatre these days.
  • The new, infectious Much Ado About Nothing, Jamie Lloyd‘s inventive and joyous revival of the Shakespeare comedy opening tonight at the Winter Garden, turns those old falling drifts of thin paper into a special effect that, for sheer exuberance, more than holds its own against the cutting-edge projections and awesome digital flimflammery delighting audiences at any number of Broadway houses this season.
  • In a recent development, of course, even a confetti squall such as this wouldn’t impress a lick if the rest of Lloyd’s production couldn’t match its energy, and fortunately for us all this Much Ado About Nothing never lacks for giddy enchantment, from the Tony-worthy performances of stars Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell to the irresistible choreography of Fabian Aloise that will likely leave audiences of this straight play convinced they’ve just witnessed one of the best new musicals on Broadway this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that outside of ticker tape parades and Newly introduced Year’s Eve in Times Square, you might be hard-pressed to think of a better, more joyous use of floating paper than the confetti that piles up nightly on the stage of Broadway‘s Winter Garden Theatre these days. We’re talking blizzards of the pink stuff, so deep that the man known for playing that Marvel trickster Loki can all but bury his superhero frame in the drifts.

The new, infectious Much Ado About Nothing, Jamie Lloyd‘s inventive and joyous revival of the Shakespeare comedy opening tonight at the Winter Garden, turns those old falling drifts of thin paper into a special effect that, for sheer exuberance, more than holds its own against the cutting-edge projections and awesome digital flimflammery delighting audiences at any number of Broadway houses this season. Related Stories News Josh Radnor & Beth Behrs To Join Broadway's 'Schmigadoon!' News Jonathan Spector's Acclaimed 'Birthright' Sets Spring Broadway Opening.

In a recent development, of course, even a confetti squall such as this wouldn’t impress a lick if the rest of Lloyd’s production couldn’t match its energy, and fortunately for us all this Much Ado About Nothing never lacks for giddy enchantment, from the Tony-worthy performances of stars Tom Hiddleston and Hayley Atwell to the irresistible choreography of Fabian Aloise that will likely leave audiences of this straight play convinced they’ve just witnessed one of the best new musicals on Broadway this season. Watch on Deadline.

Hiddleston, with his charm level cranked, and Atwell, best known to moviegoers for her Agent Carter of Marvel fame and here matching her fellow superhero beat for beat, play Benedick and Beatrice, two of Shakespeare’s most delightful characters, Loki-level tricksters who, as another character notes, engage in a “merry war” of plotting, planning and scheming in the name of love (though neither would admit to that motive, at least early on).

Lloyd, whose typically stark theatrical approach if on full view here but utilized to an effect wholly different than the shadows-and-light desolation of his A Doll’s House (starring Jessica Chastain) or Betrayal (which also paired him with Hiddleston), fashions this foray into Shakespeare as a 1990s-era dance club – at one point, the entire cast dons oversized, mascot-style headpieces (a chick, an octopus, a dog, a robot and more) suggesting so many ecstasy-fueled club kids packed into the Limelight.

The plot, of course, is the usual Shakespearean farce full of disguised identities, battles of the sexes, intricate schemes and star-crossed romances both helped and hindered by busybodies, eavesdroppers and nefarious in-laws. (In Shakespeare’s day, the word “nothing” carried a double meaning: In addition to our understood definition, “nothing” in its ye olde pronunciation carried a near-pun on the word “noting,” or gossip).

While productions of Shakespeare have long been interpreted with any number of contemporary spins and modern touches – such are the stock in trade of New York’s Shakespeare in the Park – Lloyd has come up with an approach that feels entirely fresh: Hiddleston, Atwell, the wonderful Mason Alexander Park and the rest of the cast move and sing to such jubilant dance and pop hits as Taylor Dayne’s “Tell It to My Heart,” C & C Music Factory’s “Gonna Make You Sweat (Everybody Dance Now),” Deee-Lite’s “Groove Is in the Heart,” and All-4-One’s “I Swear.” I knew we were in for a treat when Hiddleston’s Benedick and his boy crew made an entrance dancing to the Beastie Boys’ booming “Fight for Your Right (To Party).”.

If period drama set to a more-or-less contemporary soundtrack doesn’t sound all that innovative – Six and Moulin Rouge! would like a word – Lloyd and his crack creative team (and his cast, of course) see to it that we pretty much forget all other contenders. With that ever-present pink confetti, a giant inflatable heart, character-accentuating modern dress (Soutra Gilmour did both the scenic design and the party-wear costume designs) and Jon Clark’s gorgeous lighting combine to create a dazzling experience. Like any dance club worth its cover charge, the sound design (by Ben and Max Ringham) is practically a showstopper in itself, with music thumping when it needs to thump and, when we need to hear dialogue, dropping to the sort of low-level thrum you might hear on the curb outside a packed club.

Hiddleston, whose last team-up with Lloyd was the austere Betrayal, is a revelation here, adding some incredibly hot dance moves to his overflowing bag of tricks. And he’s very, very funny (watch how he ever so deadpan blows a bit of stray confetti from his lips), playing off his movie star appeal with every sidelong glance and knowing grin seemingly directed to each person in the audience (he’s not above a quick show of gratitude when his seated admirers whoop their appreciation, as if his Benedick is welcoming everyone into his scheming maneuvers).

Atwell is every bit his equal, with Beatrice’s fiery, feminist mettle rendered as the true heart and brains of this tale. Both actor and role are this productions not-so-secret weapons – and yes, Lloyd and his cast are entirely in on the Marvel appeal going on here, so much so that Hiddleston-as-Loki and Atwell-as-Carter make brief appearances in the form of standees that had the audience at the reviewed performance all but levitating.

As good as they are – and they are – newcomer (to American audiences anyway) Mason Alexander Park as the sharp-tongued Margaret nearly walks off with the show, never more so than when, mic in hand, she/they performs “Tell It To My Heart” as if placing a dance-pop diva in 16th Century Milan is no more strange than wooing your heart’s desire.

Indeed, there’s no weak link in this cast, with James Phoon’s callow young Claudio swoon-worthy when he needs to be, infuriating when he’s a jerk; Tim Steed’s meddlesome Don John a hissable villain; and Gerald Kyd’s Don Pedro – that fair-weather father to the slandered Hero (a winning Mara Huf) – an appropriately garrulous, welcoming host (until he isn’t).

The grand appeal of this production is evident in just how much Hiddleston, Atwell and their compatriots seem to be enjoying themselves, and why not? So is everyone within the clarion-call-to-groove of those thumping, galvanizing dance beats.

Title: Much Ado About NothingVenue: Broadway’s Winter Garden TheatreWritten By: Willliam ShakespeareDirected By: Jamie LloydCast: Tom Hiddleston, Hayley Atwell, Mara Huf, Mika Onyx Johnson, Gerald Kyd, Forbes Masson, Phillip Olagoke, Mason Alexander Park, James Phoon, Tim SteedRunning Time: 2 hr 20 min (including intermission).

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • Sources indicate that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

Sources indicate that advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

Sources indicate that A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In a recent development, in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

It has been revealed that “It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Industry observers note that druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly demonstrates Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

According to recent reports, he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs indicates the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

It has been revealed that despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

It has been revealed that the corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

Sources indicate that to observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most notable processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

In a recent development, that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she indicates, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, rolled out in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

It has been revealed that when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

In a recent development, it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

It has been revealed that habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” indicates Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

In a recent development, to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

According to recent reports, since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

According to recent reports, the teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

Industry observers note that but duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

According to recent reports, “Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

Recent findings suggest that if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

According to recent reports, on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

Industry observers note that but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” states Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

According to recent reports, as the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Recent findings suggest that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

Industry observers note that “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Sources indicate that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

Recent findings suggest that “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” claims Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

Sources indicate that for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

Industry observers note that with just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

According to recent reports, the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller states. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller states.

Sources indicate that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps.
  • Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable customers to generate nonconsensual nude images.
  • According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Guardian reports that three US senators have sent letters to the CEOs of Apple, Google, and Meta, demanding answers about their failure to prevent access to AI-powered ‘nudify’ apps. Here are the details.

Last month, Apple updated its App Store rules in an attempt to crack down on apps that enable customers to generate nonconsensual nude images.

According to the updated rules, apps that allow consumers to create AI-generated content must include safeguards against abuse, including tools to filter objectionable material, report offensive content, and block abusive users.

Apple also warns that apps used primarily for pornographic content or the objectification of real people may be removed from the App Store without notice.

While definitely well-intended, Apple’s changes came amid growing reports of AI-powered nudify apps, which easily allow users to generate nonconsensual intimate images.

Two months before these changes, Apple removed an app that allowed owners to create pornographic deepfakes of real people after WIRED reached out for comment, which in turn came one month after San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu demanded that Apple and Google remove several nudify apps from their app stores.

Apple also removed several apps following investigations by the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), which published reports in January and April revealing that such apps were widely available on the App Store, sometimes even appearing in sponsored search results.

Throughout these investigations, Apple has maintained that nudify apps have always been prohibited under its App Review Guidelines, and that it proactively rejects and removes apps that violate its policies, including those flagged through user reports.

Apple, of course, is not alone in this challenge, with Google facing similar criticism over their availability on the Play Store, and Meta coming under scrutiny for allowing developers to advertise these apps on Facebook and Instagram, as highlighted in the WIRED report mentioned above.

Which brings us to today’s report from The Guardian.

According to The Guardian’s exclusive report, “three Senate Democrats sent letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms.”.

A trio of US Senators say Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. They also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

The senators, namely Ron Wyden of Oregon, Ed Markey of Massachusetts, and Ben Luján of Fresh Mexico, claim that in addition to failing to remove these apps, the companies may actually be profiting from their distribution and promotion.

Commenting on the letter, both Google and Meta said they prohibit such apps or their promotion and work to detect and remove violations from their platforms, broadly echoing what Apple has repeatedly stated when reached for comment in the past over these same issues.

However, Wyden’s office argues that simply reaffirming, or in Apple’s case, updating these policies, means little if the companies continue to struggle to enforce them.

Keith Chu, the chief communications adviser and deputy policy director to Wyden, said that clarifying policies is not the same thing as enforcing them. Despite the companies reaffirming the prohibition of these apps, they continue to proliferate across Apple and Google app stores or be promoted in ads on Meta platforms, he added.

In its latest investigation, published just last month, TTP found 135 apps capable of generating nude or pornographic imagery on the App Store and the Play Store, using accounts registered to 13-year-old boys.

Additionally, researchers found that even accounts configured with parental controls were able to download these apps without requiring parental approval.

Despite Apple and Google removing the apps identified in the investigation, The Guardian noted that these apps continued to work on devices where they had already been installed.

Now, Senator Wyden warns that Congress may need to step in if the companies fail to do a better job of cracking down on these apps.

To read The Guardian’s full report, follow this link.

According to recent reports, update, 8:40 p.m. ET: In a statement to 9to5Mac, Apple said:.

“We designed the App Store to be a safe and trusted place for customers. A number of the apps in the TTP report are mainstream photo and video editing tools with legitimate, widely used functionality, and do not have nudification or deepfake capabilities. We prohibit nudify apps on the App Store, and remove developers who add capabilities like it after the App Review process — a malicious tactic known as bait-and-switch. We previously removed 28 of the apps referenced in this report before it was shared with us and have taken action on the remaining apps found to violate our rules. The report also relies on testing from older software that does not reflect current Apple safety features, including expanded protections for teens and parental controls in Screen Time that give families the ability to block kids and teens from downloading apps rated above their age.”.

Expanding on the safety features mentioned in its statement, Apple noted that teens aged 13 through 17 now have certain protections enabled by default, including web content filters, even if their parents haven’t configured any restrictions, and pointed to ⁠this support article for more information.

The firm added that children under 13 are required to use Child Accounts, and that the report relied on its previous 17+ age rating system, which was replaced last year with a more granular system that includes 13+, 16+, and 18+ ratings.

Recent findings suggest that just curious. Why doesn't someone from Apple try out the app before approving it, rather than approving it and waiting until people complain? I know there are many thousands of apps on the App store. But given that Apple makes money off most of these apps, it could surely afford to hire a staff charged with reviewing submitted apps to ensure compliance with the App store's guidelines and requirements before making them available in the App store. What am I missing here?

Apple also noted that in its report, TTP counted apps depicting people in swimwear or lingerie, which the manufacturer noted does not constitute nudification or, in itself, violate its guidelines.

According to recent reports, as for parental controls, Apple explained that, although apps that exceed a child’s configured age restrictions won’t appear in curated App Store sections, they can still be found through search, allowing children to request permission to download them through Ask to Buy. Without parental approval, the download remains blocked.

It has been revealed that apple added that Ask to Buy is supposed to require parental approval even for purchases made using gift card balances, including subscriptions. The manufacturer mentioned that if a purchase didn’t trigger an approval request, that would be unexpected behavior, and that it is investigating further.

Recent findings suggest that patch, November 19, 4:00 p.m. ET: In response to Apple’s statement, TTP director Katie Paul reached out to 9to5Mac with the following comment:.

According to recent reports, apple’s statement on nudify apps sidesteps notable concerns and leaves out key context. The manufacturer says it prohibits nudify apps but doesn’t address how its age rating system for apps contributes to the problem. TTP has shown how Apple relies on information provided by app developers to set age ratings—a self-reporting system that allows many nudify and pornographic apps to be misleadingly labeled a suitable for minors. Apple also continues to talk about removing nudify apps from the App Store, without mentioning that apps that are “removed” continue to be fully functional on people’s phones.

Industry observers note that there are many questions about Apple’s policy on nudify apps that the statement fails to address. Apple has adopted a limited definition of “nudify.” The manufacturer defines nudify apps as capable of showing someone naked, not stripping them down to a bikini or lingerie. But the company also claims it bans “creepy” and “nonconsensual intimate imagery.” What if an app is used to depict a woman in a bikini without her consent? We have asked Apple to clarify that and have not heard back.

According to recent reports, as for Apple’s comment that TTP relied on “older software,” that may refer to the fact that Apple rolled out latest child safety features in the fall. Our research was conducted in summer 2026. But many of Apple’s new features pertain to parent-supervised accounts on Apple, which have to be set up by a parent. Apple relies entirely on parents to go out of their way to locate and enable these settings. This raises obvious questions about how many people actually do this.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication concerns." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

It has been revealed that that pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be stated for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October patch. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

Recent findings suggest that it's crucial to understand that just about every manufacturer that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as swiftly as possible.

Recent findings suggest that the implications aren't specific to any one tech giant, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

It has been revealed that of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

Nearly 30 summers later, Jennifer Love Hewitt recently had an onscreen reunion with Ryan Phillippe, courtesy of an upcoming 9-1-1 crossover.

The actress, who plays 9-1-1 dispatcher Maddie Kendall in the ABC flagship series, noted that before reuniting in the crossover with 9-1-1: Nashville, she and Phillippe had “not seen each other” since starring together in the 1997 teen slasher I Know What You Did Last Summer.

“We’ve been having the best time,” Hewitt told People after they teased their reunion in an Instagram video.

Noting that it was “so great” getting to reunite with Freddie Prinze Jr. as their IKWYDLS characters Julie James and Ray Bronson in last year’s legacy sequel, Hewitt explained that working with Phillippe on 9-1-1 “was very different” as he is “newly introduced in that universe,” recently joining 9-1-1: Nashville in Season 2 as New York detective Rogue Kelly. Watch on Deadline.

Sources indicate that “I’ve been in this universe for a while,” said Hewitt, who has played Maddie since Season 2 of 9-1-1 in 2018. “It’s such a safe, lovely place to be with the best people. And he and I have not seen each other since I was 18 years old.”.

Having “never seen each other again” after wrapping the film, Hewitt noted that working together again “was a dream” and Phillippe “hadn’t — for me — changed at all,” adding that “he was the same in the most beautiful way.”.

“And it was great. When we did the first movie together, his character was so terrible to me in that movie and hated me, but he was so lovely. … all I wanted to do was drink Joy Cola and like hang out with him because he had to be so mean to me [in the movie] that I just like wanted to be his friend. And he did it,” Hewitt added. “He held that space for me still, which was really beautiful.”.

The upcoming 9-1-1 crossover with 9-1-1: Nashville comes amid the parent series’ 10th season and the spinoff’s sophomore season, airing back-to-back on Thursdays at 8/7c and 9/8c on ABC.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every once in a while, Instagram rolls out an enhancement that addresses one of its people’ most longstanding requests. Today is one of those days.

As spotted by The Verge, Instagram head Adam Mosseri confirmed today that the app will finally let customers edit a Story after publishing.

This means people will be able to add stickers and drawings, fix typos or adjust text, and even change the music without having to delete the Story and publish it again, which would mean losing any views it had already received.

The catch is that users will only have 15 minutes after publishing a Story to make changes by tapping the ellipsis button at the bottom of the screen, and then selecting “Edit story.”.

Here’s Mosseri’s post announcing the news:.

A post shared by Adam Mosseri (@mosseri).

Today’s revision is the latest in a series of changes Instagram has made this year to address longstanding user requests.

Back in March, the app introduced the ability to reorder photos and videos in a carousel after publishing. In April, it added an option to edit comments (also within 15 minutes of posting), and in June, it began letting customers manually rearrange posts on their profile grid.

More recently, Instagram also brought its free Edits video editor to the Mac, with multi-track editing, advanced color grading tools, and 4K exports.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month.
  • Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.
  • In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue mentioned Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new interview with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, Apple Music’s Zane Lowe discussed the early days of Apple Music Radio and revealed just how many people tune in each month. Here are the details.

Apple is rarely terribly specific about how many people use its services, including how many tune in to its radio stations.

In 2019, for instance, Eddy Cue mentioned Beats 1 (now Apple Music 1) had ‘tens of millions of listeners,’ but Apple has rarely provided more specific figures since.

Apple Music’s Zane Lowe, however, has now offered a more concrete figure, revealing that the service reaches over 50 million unique listeners every month:.

Sources indicate that we were never, you know, delusional enough to assume we were going to get a huge audience overnight. We’d have to build it like anyone else would have to build anything. But we’ve just got to a point in our 11 years on where we now, overall, reach over 50 million unique listeners a month, which is a really large number for us, and it’s growing exponentially and really fast.

The revelation came in a wide-ranging interview published today with Billboard’s On the Record with Kristin Robinson, where Lowe discussed Apple Music Radio’s early struggles, its approach to supporting emerging artists, and why human curation remains central to the service.

When discussing the early days at Apple Music, Lowe recalled:.

When we started the radio here, I didn’t have access or opportunity with a lot of the artists that I built relationships with from the BBC because we were unproven. And I came over here thinking, “Well, I’ve got Jimmy Iovine over here, and I’ve got Apple over here and I feel unstoppable, and who’s not going to want to come and launch this thing with us?” But it was kind of crickets… As upsetting as that was at the time, two good things came out of it. Number one, it snapped me back into the reality force field of building something from scratch. And number two, it made us focus really clearly and in a massive way on new and emerging artists.

He also mentioned some of the first artists Apple Music Radio supported, including Billie Eilish with “Ocean Eyes,” Khalid with American Teen, and Bryson Tiller with his first song.

At the time, Lowe noted, these artists were just getting started, and supporting emerging talent became a defining part of Apple Music Radio’s approach, one that continues to this day:.

Recent findings suggest that the really cool number is on our radio network. We played — this year alone — over 6,500 individual artists, which is not a commercial radio model. [Other radio networks’] playlists are very small, and the amount of plays is very great. Our playlist is gigantic. We play a lot of different artists, and over half of those 6,500 artists we’ve played in one year are new or emerging. So, think about 3,300 artists, roughly, getting played, who may be on their first song, their first EP, their first album…It’s proof of concept. It’s great.

Still on the subject of the early days at Apple Music, Lowe said “it was very clear [from the start] that that was very crucial to everybody who was responsible for bringing Apple Music to life,” adding that “serving artists and the artistic community in a way that is of most value and of most service” still drives “a lot of the decision-making” at the platform.

When the conversation turned to Apple Music’s recent rebranding, which introduced a upcoming logo physically created using sound waves from a composition by Fred again.., Lowe stated he couldn’t speak to the decisions behind it, but stressed the human element and the creative process that went into it:.

Industry observers note that we could have created that in a way that could utilize all of the tech available. We could type that into a prompt. But at the end of the day, seeing how it’s made is so much more additionally inspiring than just seeing it. It speaks to, I think, what we try to do here, which is, we love the process of what we do, and the result is a byproduct of getting to do it and loving to do it.

The matter of algorithms also came up when Lowe discussed Apple Music’s approach to music discovery, with the executive emphasizing the importance of human curation over automated recommendations:.

Well, we don’t want to say that too loudly, because someone could be like, “Wait a minute, we could cut costs here? Man, how did we not think of that!” Look, I mean, jokes aside, we’ve been incredibly fortunate, and I’ve been incredibly fortunate to take that step from the BBC into a organization and to work with people that value exactly what it is you’re describing: this idea of place and this experience of sharing things with each other, and how meaningful it is when someone shares a record with you and it comes with context. It’s a gift….

SPOILER ALERT: This post spoils the end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

The epilogue scene at the end of The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping echoes the chapter that closes Suzanne Collins’ novel of the same name.

Woody Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson appear in the final moment of the film, reprising their roles of Haymitch Abernathy, Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark, respectively, from The Hunger Games (2012), The Hunger Games: Catching Fire (2013), The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 1 (2014) and The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2 (2015).

It was known that Lawrence and Hutcherson would return for the second prequel film. Harrelson could have been a given once they were confirmed, since his character centers the latest movie. In The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which tells the villain origin story of Coriolanus Snow (Tom Blyth), Donald Sutherland’s voice was used in the end to tie the first prequel film to the original four, in which Sutherland portrayed the poisonous president. Watch on Deadline.

Industry observers note that the Sunrise scene in particular is meaningful with these three actors behind their roles because it connects the past and present, bridging the gap between The Sunrise on the Reaping and Suzanne Collins’ original trilogy of books plus their film adaptations. Haymitch, in his Quarter Quell Hunger Games, did so much to advance the rebellion that would eventually bring down Panem, the Capitol and the barbaric tradition that killed children ever year. It was Katniss who ultimately gained the momentum from this spark — symbolized by Haymitch’s flint striker and more — to topple the dystopian society and cruel reign of President Snow (Ralph Fiennes in Sunrise on the Reaping and Donald Sutherland in the first four films).

In a recent development, katniss and Peeta wish Haymitch a happy birthday in the ending scene, symbolizing that he did, in fact, reach a birthday where the sun didn’t rise on another reaping ceremony, which was his love Lenore Dove’s (Whitney Peak) dying wish. It took another 25 years after his games, which doubled the amount of tributes entered as is custom for a Quarter Quell, to overcome the tyranny. The 50th Hunger Games added a wrinkle, or extra rule, to make those games extra gruesome.

Sources indicate that by then, Peeta and Katniss, who had already somewhat thwarted the Gamemakers by threatening to each eat poisonous nightlock berries and die for there to be no victor in their 74th games, experienced a terrible Quarter Quell of their own. The 75th Hunger Games — or third Quarter Quell — involved the wrinkle that each pair of district tributes would be reaped from their existing pool of victors.

According to recent reports, the Catching Fire film made it seem like Plutarch Heavensbee (Philip Seymour Hoffman) and President Snow (Donald Sutherland) devised that wrinkle themselves to particularly torture Katniss and send her a message about her sedition. In the books, the founders of Panem left a box behind that laid out the rules of each Quarter Quell game, making it seem more like coincidence that this happened when a full-blown rebellion was close at hand.

While preparing for the third Quarter Quell, Katniss and Peeta leaned on Haymitch for his experience in the games in addition to meeting other victors turned mentors turned tributes once more like Mags (Lynn Cohen), Beetee (Jeffrey Wright), Wiress (Amanda Plummer) and others, younger versions of whom played roles in Haymitch’s story before the big Catching Fire revolt as well.

“The seeds of Haymitch Abernathy’s backstory were planted over twenty years ago when I began the original trilogy,” author Suzanne Collins wrote in a letter timed to the film’s release. “In Catching Fire, Katniss and Peeta watch the recap of his Second Quarter Quell games as he silently observes from the shadows. The Capitol had warped the true account and spun reality into vicious propaganda. For Haymitch to tell the truth about what happened would’ve been too dangerous for his tributes and too traumatic for him.”.

At the end of the snippet, Haymitch goes to the meadow to feed his flock of geese, which he raises in memory of Lenore Dove, but not before Katniss and Peeta thank him, and he in return thanks them for their teamwork in dismantling the dictatorship they lived under for so long.

Industry observers note that as for whether there could be more films in the franchise, it seems like it would come down to Collins and her decision to write another book or two. Fans have been particularly vocal about wanting more of one Finnick Odair’s first Hunger Games, and director Francis Lawrence as well as star Joseph Zada have expressed interest in diving into Plutarch’s (Jesse Plemons) story as well as the lore behind the mysterious District 13, which makes itself known in the Mockingjay books and films. Collins is known for writing these books only when she has something to say and express through them. The final scene at the end of Sunrise on the Reaping could make a great close to the story as is.

Black Friday is an excellent time to score a new pair of headphones that would otherwise be a splurge, with retailers like Amazon and Walmart already offering massive discounts on tech essentials from top brands a week ahead of the holiday. One of the early Black Friday deals that should be on your radar is the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones, a mid-range noise-canceling option that’s perfect for bass lovers and is presently 50% off, dropping to $119.99 (originally $239.99).

PCMag says they deliver “brain-rattling levels of bass” and have a comfortable fit, with generous memory foam cushioning and minimal clamping pressure that lends itself well to long listening sessions. The aesthetic is nothing to scoff at either, with a refined and modern style. It’s worth noting they also come in a hardshell zip-up case with a fabric-lined exterior.

Sources indicate that powered by 40mm dynamic drivers, they offer reliable noise cancellation with the ANC slider set to max on the companion app, which lets consumers adjust a range of controls and listening modes, including the intensity of bass. The bass boost feature is ideal for those seeking bass-heavy headphones, but may be overwhelming for those who prefer a more balanced sound.

Battery life lasts around 50 to 60 hours per charge, with Skullcandy claiming that you get four hours of listening time from around 10 minutes of charging. While brands like Bose will outperform in ANC quality, if you’re looking for noise-canceling audio gear that checks most boxes at a reasonable price point, the Skullcandy Crusher ANC 2 headphones are a smart choice, especially at over $100 off.

#3999. How Do You Land on a Moon With Almost No Gravity?
