Recent findings suggest that if you too can see the appeal of carrying all of your books with you on a device so small you'll forget it's even in your pocket, it's a great time to jump in: The recently released Xteink X4 Classic is right now 38% off for Black Friday, bringing it down to $54.87, a record-low price. Meanwhile, the smaller X3 is $55.72, or 19% off. Both are available in either "mist grey" or "space black." The discounts should last through the end of Cyber Monday on Nov. 30.

Xteink is a Chinese startup that shook up the e-reading world last year with the launch of the X4, a super bare-bones device that made up for its lack of features and usability with a cheap sub-$70 price point. Since then, a huge online community of fans has formed, sharing tips on Reddit and even coming together to crowdsource an alternate operating system that fixed a lot of early problems. Xteink swiftly followed up the X4 with a slate of other devices, including the 3.7-inch X3 and the X4 Pro, which adds a front light and touchscreen (at the cost of screen clarity and two physical buttons).

The X4 Classic and the X3 improve on the original X4 with quality-of-life upgrades like a larger battery, relocated page-turn buttons, a real-time clock, and a tilt-to-turn-page feature. They're also lighter and thinner than the X4, though there is a trade-off involved: They drop the USB-C charging port in favor of magnetic pogo pins that require a separate adapter (included).

These upgrades also increased the cost: The X4 Classic typically retails for $89, $20 more than the discontinued X4 and only $10 less than the X4 Pro, while the X3 rolled out at $79. But right now, the X4 Classic is just under $55, or around 38% off, and the X3 is about a dollar more. Either is a great option for those who prioritize crisp, readable text above the conveniences of a built-in light or touchscreen, as those add extra layers between the inner screen and outer glass. It's also crucial to understand what you're getting into: These devices support only e-books without Digital Rights Management (DRM), which means you can't use it to read your existing library of Kindle books. On the plus side, there's no longer a need to worry about flashing latest firmware if you don't want to, as the native version has been totally overhauled and is now one of your best options (though the new firmware, called "Licorice," isn't available on the X3 quite yet).

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In light of growing pushback from customers who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva today unveiled new controls that will let Free and Pro consumers choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The firm notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:.

The company states that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:.

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two newly introduced controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”.

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:.

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything newly introduced. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”.

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the firm’s design content library, Canva noted that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”.

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple is considering abandoning plans to launch an OLED iMac, according to a latest supply chain report. The news comes just weeks after the first OLED Mac was launched in the form of the new touchscreen MacBook Pro.

The organization is noted to be holding discussions with display partner Samsung about either delaying the planned launch or abandoning it altogether, with two reasons cited ….

Bring back a pro level iMac. The 27” 5k display was a very good size, make it a more accurate OLED display combined with the latest Apple Silicon, so former iMac owners have a choice where there is none now.

The all In one form factor remains convenient for labs, classrooms, creative departments, audio studios (home & pro), etc.

Keep the non OLED 24” display format positioned as a consumer model, plus lower its cost and you will see a sales uptick.

Apple’s journey into OLED screens began with the Apple Watch while other products were still using IPS LCD. The company subsequently switched to OLED for some iPhones and iPads before a long-awaited launch of the first OLED MacBook Pro back in October.

It was expected that the manufacturer would gradually transition to OLED across the full range of Macs over time. However, this process was expected to take a number of years, with the iMac not likely to join the party until 2029 or 2030.

The Elec today reports that the move may be delayed even further or even abandoned altogether, for two reasons: cost and demand.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer is said to be discussing a potential delay or cancellation of the project with Samsung Display. High OLED panel costs and weak sales of existing OLED-equipped products are believed to be factors behind the reconsideration […].

The biggest factor behind the review is cost. The iMac sells in smaller volumes than smartphones or laptops, making it difficult to maintain competitive pricing if expensive OLED panels are adopted. Weak sales of the OLED iPad Pro are also believed to have influenced the decision.

Industry observers note that the report suggests that incoming CEO John Ternus has been reviewing the commercial viability of upgrading more products to OLED. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Model ML co-founders Chaz and Arnie Englander in London.

Model ML, a London startup that builds AI agents for bankers, consultants and investors, has raised $250m at a $1.5bn valuation. General Atlantic and QED Investors co-led the Series B round, the firm said on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that evolution Equity Partners, Airtree, Forestay Capital, Y Combinator, FT Partners, Latitude, Inception Fund and 13Books Capital also took part. The round takes Model ML’s total funding to $350m. FT Partners led its $75m Series A in November 2025, and HSBC Asset Management invested in August.

Industry observers note that in the third quarter, Model ML’s annual recurring revenue grew 12 times year on year and its daily active customers rose 26 times, the company noted. It will use the money to grow its research and engineering teams in London and Newly introduced York.

In a recent development, brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander founded Model ML in 2023, Bloomberg reported. They previously co-founded Fat Llama, a rental marketplace that Sweden’s Hygglo bought for $41.5m in 2022, TechCrunch reported.

Each user gets an agent that runs on the firm’s own systems and data. When news breaks on a company a banker covers, the agent judges whether it matters and prepares the analysis in the firm’s formats. It works in tools such as Excel and PowerPoint to build pitch decks and due diligence reports.

In a recent development, “AI should do more than give you another answer or notification. It should understand your work and get things done,” noted Chaz Englander, Model ML’s co-founder and CEO.

It has been revealed that model ML sends each task to the AI model that suits it best. A growing share runs on its own fine-tuned open-source models. On the work they handle, these cost 2% as much as frontier models and are in most cases five times faster, the tech giant said. It added that customer data is never used to train AI models.

Banks have tied job cuts to AI. Barclays said in October it would cut 5,000 jobs, and Standard Chartered prepares to cut 7,800 jobs in back-office roles by 2030. Englander played down the idea that Model ML is mainly a way to cut costs.

“The average age of a Model ML user is 33 years old, not 23 years old,” Englander told Bloomberg. “These tools are no longer productivity and efficiency tools. They’re revenue generative.”.

Revenue is split fairly evenly across banks, consulting firms and asset managers, he said. Model ML’s rivals include Newly introduced York’s Rogo, which raised $160m at a $2bn valuation in April. OpenAI and Anthropic also sell AI tools to financial professionals.

#3961. UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

UK court rules Apple can share the top secret order everyone already knew

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (759 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.
  • Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the glitch ….
  • The story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal – essentially a British court that deals with complaints about state surveillance – has ruled that Apple is allowed to reveal a secret order it received from the UK government.

Apple had already found a clever way to alert British customers to the classified order without breaking the law, but it can now confirm what we all already knew, and talk openly about the glitch ….

The story centers on Apple’s introduction of the Advanced Data Protection (ADP) privacy feature back in 2022. This extended end-to-end encryption to almost all your iCloud data, meaning Apple has no access, and therefore cannot grant access to any government agencies who come knocking on its door.

In a recent development, the feature is off by default because it means Apple cannot help you access any of your data if, for example, you forget your iCloud password. However, those who want to maximize the privacy of their iCloud account can enable it.

Industry observers note that in 2025, the British government ordered Apple to create a backdoor to allow access by security services and law enforcement. Even worse, the order was issued under legislation that prohibits companies from revealing that they have received this demand.

It has been revealed that this would have meant that British customers who enabled ADP would think that their data was safe when in fact it wasn’t. As we’ve mentioned many times before, any backdoor created for use by the good guys is vulnerable to discovery and exploitation by the bad guys.

It would have been illegal for Apple to reveal that it had been instructed to compromise the privacy of customer data, but the tech giant found a clever way to effectively communicate this without breaking the law. Apple confirmed it was withdrawing ADP from the UK without explaining its reason.

Sources indicate that “Apple can no longer offer Advanced Data Protection (ADP) in the United Kingdom to latest customers and current UK users will eventually need to disable this security feature. ADP protects iCloud data with end-to-end encryption, which means the data can only be decrypted by the user who owns it, and only on their trusted devices. We are gravely disappointed that the protections provided by ADP will not be available to our customers in the UK […] As we have said many times before, we have never built a backdoor or master key to any of our products or services and we never will.”.

Tell me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP without telling me you’ve been ordered to create a backdoor to ADP ….

At this point, it was an open secret. However, ridiculously, despite the fact that everyone in the security and privacy field knew about it and was talking about it, Apple was still not allowed to officially confirm it.

The iPhone maker asked the Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) to allow it to openly discuss the order, with privacy campaigners backing this call. The Financial Times reports that the court has now ruled in Apple’s favor.

Sources indicate that the UK government must admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled […] The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal stated. The ruling means that […] “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.

One of the great ironies is that most people had never heard of ADP until the government effectively made it headline news in the tech press three years after it introduced – a classic example of the Streisand Effect.

In a recent development, this ruling is a win both for transparency and commonsense. To be clear, the actual requirement for a backdoor remains in place, but this can now be challenged in open court.

Industry observers note that amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

It has been revealed that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save massive on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the organization introduced a newly introduced model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

Sources indicate that if you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

Sources indicate that if you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

If you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is at the moment $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

According to recent reports, the upcoming Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

Sources indicate that if you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Discounted $30 to $229.99 at Best Buy, it's currently pricier than the Kindle Colorsoft, but you get a bit more for your money. While most of the specs are similar (they both use the same Kaleido 3 screen and offer 32GB of storage), the Kobo supports a stylus, so you can jot down notes in your books or keep a digital journal. It also has physical page-turn buttons, which the Colorsoft lacks.

Industry observers note that if you don't want to be tied to the Amazon ecosystem and/or you're looking for a device that's a bit more portable, consider the Viwoods AiPaper Reader, at the moment marked down to $200, its lowest price ever. It's got a 6.13-inch screen, so it's the same size and shape as your phone, and it has a crisp e-ink screen with a strong (if not temperature-adjustable) front light and 128GB of onboard storage. The best part is, it runs on an open Android system, so you can install multiple reading apps, including Kindle, Nook, Kobo, and Libby, and keep all of your books in one place. (Check out my review of the Viwoods AiPaper Reader for more—it's a nifty little device.).

If you don't have a large Kindle library, you're moderately tech-savvy, and you praise portability above all else, I can't recommend Xteink's line of e-readers more highly. The 4.3-inch Xteink X4 Classic is at its lowest price ever, coming in at just under $55, around $34 off the list price. Meanwhile, the smaller 3.7-inch Xteink X3 is about a dollar more; that's a less-generous 19% discount. I own both, and while the Classic is definitely worth the current sale price, I actually prefer the form factor of the smaller X3 (currently $55.72), which is about the size of a library card.

If you're feeling tentative about trusting a seemingly no-name Chinese tech brand, read more about the devices in my review, or listen to the collected wisdom of the tens of thousands of people in the bustling r/xteink Reddit group.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

It has been revealed that follow our Black Friday coverage for the latest and best deals our team finds. Another good tip is to only buy what you need. It sounds simple, but making a list of the things you want before jumping into a sale with millions of products helps you focus and make smarter decisions.

Recent findings suggest that no. If you find the product you're looking for with a major discount right now, get it. It's not likely to drop any lower, but it could always run out of stock. Take advantage of price matching or guarantees instead of waiting. Remember, you can always return products later if you change your mind. For the majority of products, the deal from Black Friday will be the same one on Cyber Monday.

#3959. Weight-Space Programming builds neural networks like a 1990s researcher

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2918 w)

Weight-Space Programming builds neural networks like a 1990s researcher

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Notesbylex

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The writing aspect of WSP turns out to be quite a history lesson.
  • Weight-Space Programming still has me pretty intrigued.
  • In a recent development, in the original blog post, beyond the reading and editing experiments, the authors had GPT-6 Astra build a network to play Go from scratch, then improve it by playing practice games, and editing the weights based on analysis of its losses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The writing aspect of WSP turns out to be quite a history lesson.

Weight-Space Programming still has me pretty intrigued. The basic idea is that frontier LLMs can read, write and edit the weights of neural networks. There's nuance to what's going on, but it feels like there's a lot of new ground to explore.

In a recent development, in the original blog post, beyond the reading and editing experiments, the authors had GPT-6 Astra build a network to play Go from scratch, then improve it by playing practice games, and editing the weights based on analysis of its losses. That loop of writing, testing and editing feels like a newly introduced way to train a network, something like LLM Descent. But is it?

In this article, I run my own weight-writing experiment with Claude Fable 5.2 on a familiar image classification problem. Look closely at what the model builds, and it turns out to be an interesting lesson in historical model-building techniques. With that latest lens on weight-space programming, I also study the Go network that Astra built in the original article, and find something very similar.

Recent findings suggest that MNIST is the OG image classification problem. The goal is to label each handwritten digit, 0 to 9.

In a recent development, similar to the Go test in the original Weight-Space Programming post, I built a test with a fixed CNN, then prompted Claude to write code that sets all its weights from scratch, with a few rules that include no fitting, regression, or searching. Drawing filters and templates by hand, from formulas or strokes, is explicitly allowed.

According to recent reports, it's a considerably stricter setup than Astra had for Go, with no PyTorch and no practice games, only its training loss, accuracy and confusion matrix after each attempt. The tests in this blog post were run with Claude Fable 5.2, which performed much better than Opus 5.5.

Claude starts with no weights at all, and has to set every one of this network's 5,994 weights "by hand":.

You can read the whole prompt on GitHub.

Sources indicate that claude's code runs in a sandbox that can only import NumPy, SciPy and math. Once it returns the weights, a test harness runs the network on the training and test images.

Industry observers note that claude has up to 50 steps, and at each one it sees all the feedback so far. The training set is 10,000 images from MNIST's official training split. Claude never sees the 10,000 official test images or how it scores on them, and the network with the lowest training loss gives us the final test score.

Here's an example of the feedback it gets after its first attempt:.

Though I have early stopping configured to stop when the training loss stops improving, all three runs descend for the full 50 steps, still improving when they run out, and land around 90% on the test set. Amazingly, that's close to where a training run with Adam gets to after 50 gradient steps.

In 1998, LeCun's paper that introduced MNIST described that era's approaches thus far as "a fixed feature extractor and a trainable classifier", where the feature extractor "is often entirely hand crafted" (LeCun et al., 1998). Accuracy, he wrote, "is largely determined by the ability of the designer to come up with an appropriate set of features", which is "a daunting task which, unfortunately, must be redone for each fresh problem.".

In a recent development, that daunting task is exactly what Claude takes on. All three runs built the same kind of pipeline, though not from the same parts:.

The first step at which each run's network uses the technique.

Let's follow run 1, step by step, based on Claude's replies and reasoning. It's the best of the three, at 91.3%, but the other two follow a similar path, measuring their way from hand-drawn templates to a classifier.

Claude starts like a 1990s computer vision engineer. Its first layer is a set of line detectors at four angles, written from formulas. They're cousins of the Sobel filter, a classic way to find edges in an image, which 1990s digit recognisers started with (Favata and Srikantan, 1996).

Each detector is a 5×5 grid of weights in the first convolutional layer. The way a conv layer works is that each filter slides across the image, multiplying the 25 pixels under it by its 25 weights and adding them up, so it scores high wherever there's a stroke at its angle, and zero on blank paper. Fable fills in four of the layer's eight filters this way and leaves the other four at zero for later.

Its second layer adds up each detector's map over patches of the image, so every image ends up as a 4×4 grid of cells saying which stroke directions appear in each.

Then it draws each digit by hand, as a few strokes in code, and turns each drawing into the same kind of grid: how likely each stroke direction is in each cell. Those tables become the final layer's weights, so it scores every image against all ten tables.

The final layer is a 10 by 256 grid of weights, with one row for each digit's table.

The weights are the log-odds of that table, scaled down by a temperature.

The log-odds turn each probability into a score that can simply be added up, and the temperature turns all the scores down, so the network isn't overconfident.

This is template matching - one of the oldest approaches in character recognition (Mori et al., 1992). The scoring works like naive Bayes, which treats each feature as separate evidence for each digit. Bayesian rules for reading characters go back to 1957 (Chow, 1957).

Its first network gets 71% on the test set. Redrawing the digits the confusion matrix claims are wrong brings it to 77%.

At step 3, it fills its four empty filters with corner detectors, and combines them in conv2's empty channels into a loop detector: four corners around a blank middle.

A researcher might have studied the digits to see where their features go wrong. We haven't given Claude the ability to do that in this test, but at step 4, it tries an interesting approach, where it stops classifying for a step and tests a loop detector (a feature for closed loops, like the ones in 0, 6, 8 and 9) on its own:.

I cannot tell that from a confusion matrix where everything is mixed together, so this step tests the detector on its own, like a unit test.

Recent findings suggest that it rewires the output layer so that each "predicted digit" means how strongly, and where, the loop detector fired. Each row of the confusion matrix then becomes a histogram of the loop detector for one true digit. One step later, it knows the detector fires on 83% of 8s. At steps 6 and 7, it tests its own drawings the same way, putting variants of each digit head to head.

In a way, this is kinda cheating, but then again it doesn't break the rules. The code doesn't run the network or fit anything, or even see an image. And hey: the test set is untouched, so the scores are still honest.

It has been revealed that next, it turns the corner detectors inside its loop detector into features of their own: four corner shapes where strokes meet (┌ ┐ └ ┘). It frees four of conv2's loop channels to carry the corner maps, and gives the final layer a weight for each corner in each half of the image. Handwriting recognisers relied on shape features like these (Trier et al., 1996) (Favata and Srikantan, 1996). At first it guesses how often each one reveals up in each digit. When that stalls at about 81%, it measures them instead, three steps in a row, and sets their weights from the results.

Three measurement steps on the corners gave more than many steps of guessing, and they showed that some of my hand-drawn expectations were far off.

According to recent reports, by step 18, it's at 83%. Pretty incredible, if you ask me.

From here on, the convolution layers never change. Every measurement, and every fix, happens in the final layer.

So it measures everything else too. Over the next twelve steps, it reads out how often each of its 32 stroke features fires on each digit, three at a time. At step 24, it plugs in the first fifteen measurements to check they help, and accuracy jumps from 83% to 88%.

At step 31, it throws its hand-drawn templates away completely.

rebuild the whole classifier from measured rates: 32 orientation cells, 8 corner zones and the loop detector. No hand-drawn stroke templates remain in the final layer.

What's left is a naive Bayes-style classifier, with every probability measured from the training set, one feature at a time, through the confusion matrix. In other words, it's fitting a classifier by hand. It reaches 89%, then 90% after tuning a few global settings. Then it spends steps 36 to 40 measuring the half of the stroke grid it hadn't covered yet.

Sources indicate that the last ten steps are fine-tuning by hand, scaling groups of the final layer's weights up and down to decide how much to trust each kind of evidence and how confident its predictions should be. It also keeps track of exactly how it will be scored.

if this step does not beat 0.3111, step 48 is the one that gets scored.

It finishes at 91.3% on the test set, which is roughly where 50 steps of training with Adam gets us. It's not quite a like-for-like comparison, though: Adam's 50 steps see 64 images each, 3,200 in total, while Claude gets scores over all 10,000 training images at every step.

Opus 5.5 reaches for the same toolbox, with stroke detectors, hand-drawn templates, nearest centroid (picking the closest template), naive Bayes, and loop and endpoint detectors. The difference seems to be how much it measures. Fable spent far more steps measuring than Opus, which tended to prefer guessing. Opus also didn't manage to get a score beyond 74% on the test set. I also ran a few tests with Opus 5.5 that gave the model more feedback, including example digits, but they didn't make much difference, so I've left them out of this post.

Each step folder has the reply, thinking summary, code and metrics.

I ran the same test on photos from Kaggle's famous Dogs vs. Cats competition, with an image size of 64x64, using a slightly bigger fixed CNN (24,898 weights), the same rules and the same stopping rule. Here we can see some of the limitations of the hand-crafted feature approach, and some of the potential upper bounds of "weight-space programming".

Sources indicate that fable 5.2 takes the same initial approach as it did on MNIST, building a bank of hand-designed detectors, including pointed ears, an eyes-and-nose triangle and grass, then testing some of them one at a time. But those ideas don't bear much fruit:.

The ear probe highlighted the opposite of my guess.

Industry observers note that what does work is studying properties of the photo rather than the animal: dog photos have more green (grass and outdoor scenes), more texture, and more vertical edges. Its best network, at step 9, uses just those three. Nothing it adds after that does better, so the run stops at step 17.

It lands at 61.6% on the test set, where a coin flip gets 50%. It actually beats 500 steps of Adam (55%), but this small network is slow to train, and after 5,000 steps Adam reaches 74%. Fable's run was also very expensive, at $8.08 for 17 steps.

With this new perspective on how Weight-Space Programming builds an image classification model by hand-crafting it using known pre-deep-learning techniques, let's look at the Go network Astra built in the original article and see if there are any parallels.

In the original article, Astra was given a 9x9 Go network with 1.5M parameters, all set to zero. It had a Python sandbox, but wasn't allowed to train, fit or search, and was told to make the network play Go as well as it could. In most runs, it could also use "passes": each pass plays a batch of up to 128 practice games and shows it the results. The authors ran it four times, with budgets of 0, 10, 25 and 50 passes.

Sources indicate that and that seemed to work really well. With 50 passes, the Astra-built network beat two small networks trained with reinforcement learning (PPO) in over 80% of games, and beat one of the same size, trained on 20.5 million games, most of the time. Actually, even with no practice games played at all, Astra managed to write a network that still won over half its games against the smaller networks (Takehi et al., 2026).

Let's dig deeper into this result to try to understand what's going on.

Astra describes the final solution in its output:.

The hand-coded, symmetry-preserving policy combines approximate group-liberty propagation, captures, connected-group rescues, self-atari and eye avoidance, and ko/snapback risk suppression.

In a recent development, I must disclose here that I don't know much about Go, or how Go-winning models are built. So this section was largely put together in consultation with Opus 5.5.

According to recent reports, apparently, every item on that list is a staple of classical Go programs, including counting "liberties" to tell which groups can be captured, recognising eyes to tell which groups live, handling ko, and estimating territory with an influence function, where each stone radiates influence that fades with distance. The first Go programs were built entirely on influence functions (Bouzy and Cazenave, 2001) (Müller, 2002).

Additionally, behind those 1.48 million weights is a config of 26 hand-set numbers, compiled into the network by a design script:.

According to recent reports, the design script builds the network layer by layer, like a hand-written board analysis. It starts with layer 1, which counts each stone's liberties. Then layers 2 and 3 spread that evidence through connected stones. Next, layer 4 flags groups in atari and self-atari. After that, layer 5 scores captures and rescues. And, finally, layer 6 combines tactics with connection, territory and eyes. The 26 numbers mostly set how much each rule counts.

Its improvement from practice games was nudging those numbers by hand, and adding five newly introduced rules along the way, such as a penalty for ko repetition.

Play, diagnose, add a rule or retune one, which is basically how rule-based Go programs were built for decades (Müller, 2002), and shares a lot of parallels with the image classification approach described in the first section.

Industry observers note that so the paper's most impressive from-scratch network is a rule-based Go program, compiled into weights. That is truly an incredible feat of engineering: a hand-written program that beats a PPO network trained on 20.5 million games.

In a recent development, in this article, we've taken a closer look at how weight-space programming "writes" networks, leaving aside its other findings about reading and editing weights. On MNIST and in Go, the models drew on their extensive knowledge of classical techniques and combined them in sophisticated ways, guided by careful measurement of the feedback they were given. On harder problems like cats vs dogs, though, the limits of hand-crafted features start to show.

Industry observers note that so, from these experiments at least, LLMs aren't so much "writing in weight-space" as brilliantly chaining together hand-designed techniques. And I think there's a second takeaway: there's a lot to learn from watching LLMs work. They were trained on human knowledge, and now, it seems, they have a lot to teach us.

Everything is in the experiments repo: the prompts, every reply and thinking summary, the code and weights from every step, the MNIST protocol and the cats vs dogs run.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that apple’s fresh HomeView just rolled out last Friday, but some early adopters reported issues with Siri AI in their first days of use. Apple shipped fixes in HomeView 27.2.1 yesterday, but it also confirmed the iOS 27.3 beta is responsible for some of the problems.

Yesterday Apple released its first post-launch software enhancement for HomeView, less than a week after the product debuted.

Per the manufacturer’s official release notes, HomeView 27.2.1 focuses on bug fixes, including a fix for the following matter:.

Pairing with an iPhone or iPad running the iOS or iPadOS 27.3 beta may cause Siri requests to fail.

Sources indicate that it’s unknown how many reports of Siri complications on HomeView can be attributed to the iOS 27.3 beta. However, it wouldn’t surprise me if many of the reports were from beta users. That’s in part because early HomeView reviewers didn’t seem to have the same problems.

With HomeView 27.2.1 now available, those problems should hopefully be taken care of. However, if you’re on the iOS 27.3 beta, there’s a newly introduced matter you’ll need to deal with temporarily.

As discovered by pdfu, if you try to make a Personal Content request on an iPhone running iOS 27.3, Siri in HomeView 27.2.1 now claims: “I can’t help with that because your personal device is on newer software.”.

If you’re on iOS 27.3, Siri on HomeView can’t use your iPhone for personal context, likely until December.HomeView won’t send Siri requests to an iPhone on newer software. Without a HomeView update, your only option is iOS 27.2.x.On-device requests like timers still work. https://t.co/8UbRs7z496.

According to recent reports, it’s understandable that issues might arise from having iOS and HomeView software that’s out of sync. Unfortunately though, there’s no beta software available for HomeView at the moment.

That means unless Apple releases a beta soon, people might have to wait until the public launch of HomeView 27.3 in December to get Personal Content features back.

Google’s Gemini assistant can now take over tasks on a Mac, clicking through apps, typing and filling in forms for you. Google unveiled on Thursday that computer use is rolling out in the Gemini app for Mac.

You describe a task, and Gemini works through it across local files, desktop apps and websites. It runs in a separate background window with a live preview in the chat, so your screen and cursor stay free. You choose which apps it can use, can pause it, and must approve key actions.

Sources indicate that google’s examples include pulling weights and addresses from PDFs into a shipping quote form, and turning dashboard data into a Google Slides deck. It can also batch-edit photos or prepare resale listings from pictures in a folder.

It has been revealed that google warns that Gemini can make mistakes, including permanently deleting files or sharing them with others. It is designed to ask permission first, and it can only see folders you connect. Backups of changed files are deleted after 24 hours or when you start a upcoming task.

It has been revealed that google is also building Gemini into the operating system of its Googlebook laptops, as rivals race to put agents on the desktop. OpenAI’s ChatGPT can log your keystrokes on a Mac to build its memory. Agents built on the OpenClaw framework have helped drive Mac mini demand.

  • Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).
  • A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our relationships are foundational to our lives—our sense of safety and how we understand the world around us. When someone close to us suddenly, imperceptibly shifts, it can be unsettling, especially because you can’t be sure what’s changed or why. Those are the waters where Hulu’s Phony swims, delivering a perfectly pitched dramedy about a teenager (Sam Nivola) who emerges from a brief coma convinced that his mother (a pitch-perfect Connie Britton) has been replaced with a double. If you loved the series (and similar demonstrates) and you’re looking for more intriguing stories about doubles and impostors close to home, you should definitely watch Goodnight Mommy.

Goodnight Mommy definitely leans into the psychological horror aspect of an impostor mother much, much harder than Phony, but it’s just a deeper dive into the show’s darker implications (and, fair warning, this movie is dark).

A woman identified only as Mother returns from having cosmetic surgery with her face totally enveloped in bandages, and her twin sons observe strange differences in her behavior that convince them she isn’t their real mother—she appears to ignore one of her sons completely, and disciplines them much more harshly than before. The boys also find clues that bolster their fears, including a photograph showing their mother posing with a woman dressed identically to her.

Industry observers note that the boys’ attempts to force her to confess rapidly descend into a kind of madness, ultimately leading them to tie her to the bed in an effort to force her to admit she’s not their real mother. It all leads to a reveal as affecting as Phony’s ultimate explanation (albeit a lot more grim and violent). The film goes way harder than the series, but if you were totally into the premise, this is the more horrifying version you’ll want to see. The original film is German; there was a 2022 remake starring Naomi Watts, and while it's pretty good, the original is the right choice. Stream Goodnight Mommy on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more impostor stories that dig into the psychological and emotional impact of suspecting someone has been replaced? Here are a few more movies that dig into the concept.

Recent findings suggest that the Hole in the Ground offers an inversion: A mother who becomes convinced that her son has been replaced by an impostor. Firmly in the supernatural horror genre, the story still plays the same game with the viewer: Is Sarah (Seána Kerslake) crazy, or has her son, Chris (James Quinn Markey), been replaced by a creature living in the woods near their home? It’s got the same disturbing energy as Sarah struggles with how much her son’s changed behavior is her own psychological projection and how much is clear evidence that he’s no longer the same person—or, possibly, even the same species. Stream The Hole in the Ground on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, taking a slightly more literary approach (it’s based on a novella by Fyodor Dostoyevsky), The Double explores what happens if you find yourself replaced by a doppelgänger. Simon (Jesse Eisenberg) is a nonentity—ignored at work, lonely, and silently longing for the girl living across the street, Hannah (Mia Wasikowska). One day, a upcoming employee named James appears at Simon’s job—and James looks exactly like Simon. But James is assertive, confident, and charming, sending Simon into a spiral. As the two versions slide into a battle for dominance, Simon finds himself turning to increasingly deranged moves to rid himself of the new and improved version of himself. If you loved the psychological implications that Phony explores, check out The Double. Stream The Double on Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

On one level, Denis Villeneuve’s 2013 film is about a college professor named Adam (Jake Gyllenhaal) who discovers an actor named Anthony who looks exactly like him (also played by Gyllenhaal). When he tracks his double down, their lives merge in messy ways, ending in tragedy and one of the most striking (and confusing) final shots in cinema history. On another level, Enemy is a deft trick, exploring someone’s subconscious using dream logic and misdirection. If the best part about Phony was the disorienting sense that a secret just under the surface will explain everything, Enemy is the perfect choice. Stream Enemy on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a deeper, crazier, and more terrifying story about doubles, Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 film is a terrific choice. Inspired in part by his own feelings in the wake of a painful divorce, the story follows Mark (Sam Neil), a spy who returns to West Berlin at the height of the Cold War only to find out his wife, Anna (Isabelle Adjani), has been having an affair and wants a divorce. But Anna’s behavior becomes increasingly strange, and then Mark meets their son’s teacher, Helen, who looks just like Anna. And that’s before Anna kind of ... grows a replacement Mark from a tentacled creature kept in her bathroom (and that’s just the beginning of how weird this movie gets), resulting in two doubles. How much of the film is meant literally and how much simply represents the trauma of romantic betrayal and divorce is up to you, but Possession will definitely leave a mark. Stream Possession on Shudder, Kanopy, or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that obsession looks at the Doppelgänger Effect from a different perspective. Cliff Robertson plays Michael Courtland, a wealthy businessman whose wife (Geneviève Bujold) and young daughter, Amy (Wanda Blackman), are kidnapped in 1959. When he follows police advice against delivering the ransom, both appear to be killed in an explosion. Courtland spends the next 16 years hating himself, until he encounters a young woman, Sandra (also Bujold), who looks almost exactly like his late wife. He works to make Sandra look as much like his wife as possible, and eventually proposes—but then Sandra is kidnapped in precisely the same way as his wife and daughter sixteen years before. This all leads to a head-spinning series of reveals and a twist that echoes the Hitchcock classic Vertigo. Rent Obsession on Prime Video.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps.
  • In a recent development, the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027.
  • According to recent reports, “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft is saying goodbye to its task management service To Do, including the Mac and iOS apps. Here’s what users need to know.

In a recent development, the last day to use the To Do apps is June 30, 2027. That date also applies to Windows, Android, and the web. The underlying service and sync support will retire later, according to Microsoft’s support document.

According to recent reports, “Microsoft To Do is retiring,” Microsoft explains. “For work or school accounts, Microsoft Planner will be the destination for managing personal work tasks alongside assigned work. The updated My tasks experience begins rolling out in December 2026.”.

Industry observers note that on the Mac, you can use Planner on the web or in Teams. Microsoft explicitly states it has no prepares for a native Mac app.

Industry observers note that you can still see your existing To Do tasks in Planner through June 30, but your tasks and lists won’t carry over. Microsoft plans to offer an export option before the apps retire.

Planner doesn’t support personal Microsoft accounts however. If that’s how you use To Do, you’ll need to pick another task manager, even if you pay for Microsoft 365 Personal or Family, according to the company.

The June shutdown will end a run of just over a decade for To Do on Apple platforms. Microsoft bought the company behind Wunderlist in 2015 and released the first iPhone preview of To Do in April 2017.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft has been trying to make Teams as the super app for some time now, as Planner is integrated into Teams. Teams is one of the prime examples of why super apps are terrible, with a bloated, web app-like experience.

Looking for a proper replacement? Apple’s built-in Reminders app can keep lists in sync between Apple devices, including a grocery list you share with family through iCloud.

If you liked To Do because it worked across platforms, Todoist has apps for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Windows, and Android.

Does this sunsetting affect you? Were you a Wunderlist user back in the day? Share your thoughts in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, right now the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and customers who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple states the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

Industry observers note that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Recent findings suggest that yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

  • Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next.
  • Industry observers note that to examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature.

Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.

Industry observers note that to examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence, whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum.

In a recent development, ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades).

It has been revealed that interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision.

Yet knowing those upper limits doesnât tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, itâs hard to predict how capable a âgood enoughâ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human.

Industry observers note that what we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both todayâs AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted.

Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient.

Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute, driven by three compounding factors:.

Recent findings suggest that multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world.

At the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year. A cognitive workload that can be performed by todayâs AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023.

It has been revealed that extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised. Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services.

Is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? Itâs certainly not a given, but practical ceilings on compute build-out, and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of todayâs AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now.

It has been revealed that would cognitive industrialization alone be enough to achieve ASI? If we froze other dimensions of AI progress and only scaled up todayâs AIs in speed and number, the result might not even count as full AGI: there may still be cognitive tasks that AI cannot do without human help. Nonetheless, sheer scale can have a quality of its own. Suppose that we do achieve broadly human-level AI. Then there is clearly a major difference between human-level AIs that are slow and expensive to run, and a world where billions of agents act much faster than humans. That quantitative leap in speed and scale might itself be enough to bridge the qualitative gap from AGI to (weak) ASI.

Unlike humans, digital intelligence directly benefits from more and faster compute in several fundamental ways:.

Dramatically more efficient AI and larger compute stocks can scale up the speed and number of AI agents at a given capability level. But some missing capabilities may be hard - or impossible - to patch over with sheer volume. While Einstein did figure out general relativity, a conference of one hundred thousand Ptolemaic astronomers probably wouldnât have.

AI could follow four potential technological pathways to unlock previously unavailable cognitive capabilities. (For an in-depth discussion, see our From AGI to ASI report.).

Sources indicate that so far, qualitative capabilities have improved with remarkable consistency alongside model and data scale. This trend is captured by scaling laws that relate model performance to training compute, training data, and more recently, test-time compute (giving a model extra computing power to reason through a problem before answering).

It has been revealed that these scaling âlaws,â however, are extrapolations of observed trends that hold only within familiar boundaries, such as a particular model architecture, type of training data, and family of evaluations. They canât confidently predict the scale required for AGI or ASI, but we can identify potential bottlenecks to continued scaling of models and data:.

Todayâs dominant AI paradigm is to train large transformers to predict the next symbol in a long sequence across vast datasets, then refine them to learn to reason and follow instructions, and give them extra test-time compute. Recent research suggests this paradigm can, in principle, produce models that can run complex algorithms, including powerful learning algorithms, via their prompts - that is, without requiring retraining. This is a key ingredient for building AI systems at the theoretical upper limit of intelligence.

According to recent reports, but todayâs models fall short of humans on a few fundamental dimensions, including continual learning, certain forms of world modeling, decision-making, and sample efficiency - meaning that AI models need to be initially trained on much more data than humans to reach roughly the same intelligence level. They may also be missing the ability to invent genuinely newly introduced concepts and abstractions rather than recombining existing ones. Researchers are divided on whether these problems can be solved with simple extensions and evolutions of todayâs paradigm, or whether reaching ASI will require truly deep technological paradigm shifts.

Human corporations, markets, and research communities solve problems that no individual could tackle alone. Similarly, coordinating thousands or millions of AGI instances into "group agents" or virtual agent economies could produce collective superintelligence. What is unclear today is how AI group intelligence could scale as we add more agents and compute, depending on how agents are organized. That is, we need multi-agent scaling laws. Early research finds clear intelligence gains in some tasks, but coordination inefficiencies still lead to diminishing returns as the population size grows.

According to recent reports, less obviously, steering large agent collectives will require robust institutional design and organizational mechanisms, including defenses against accidental or intentional misinformation spread, manipulation, and collusion. Experiments with agent swarms are already demonstrating how swiftly these dynamics can emerge, with individual agents learning to cheat and others acting as whistleblowers to expose them.

According to recent reports, finally, AI systems could begin automating improvements to future generations of AI - a process known as recursive self-improvement (RSI) that was first discussed by I. J. Good and Ray Solomonoff.

Unlike typical technological development, improvements to AI could directly speed up subsequent gains, leading to an accelerating rate of progress. However, further improvements in research tend to be âharder to findâ - more and more effort is required to maintain the same rate of improvement across technologies. Whether RSI leads to ârunawayâ progress is largely an empirical question.

RSI is not a single process. It can operate via improvements to code and designs - from model architectures and training algorithms to chip layouts. It can also operate through data, by spending compute at deployment to produce improved results and outputs that can be reused to train future models. AlphaZero self-improved purely in this data driven way to reach superhuman performance.

It has been revealed that finally, RSI can play out at the group level by dividing labor and specializing roles in an agent collective. A group of coordinated specialists can achieve more than the sum of what they could achieve as isolated generalists, in turn becoming more effective at finding further improvements. Instead of just scaling up a team with fixed roles, larger and more efficient collectives enable newly introduced types of specialization that were previously unviable - much like how a multi-cellular organism can support specialized organs like a heart or a brain, as opposed to a single-celled organism that perform all survival functions on its own.

These three RSI mechanisms mirror evolutionary processes that drove the growth of human cognitive capabilities: genetic (code and design), cultural (data), and social evolution (group specialization through cooperation).

Industry observers note that importantly, RSI loops can easily stall or degenerate if the feedback guiding them is poor. Pursuing ASI via recursive self-improvement therefore requires evaluation methods that can be rapidly scaled into the superhuman regime, where even large groups of humans can't easily assess AI outputs. Accordingly, RSI should advance fastest in domains that allow for automated verification without humans in the loop, such as mathematical proofs, while other domains might lag behind or taper off sooner.

Industry observers note that these pathways to ASI are not mutually exclusive - in fact, they compound on one another. If progress on one stalls, economic and geopolitical competition will likely shift effort toward the others. Even if RSI doesnât result in runaway gains, continued scaling in training data, speed, efficiency, and coordination could still drive rapid progress well beyond human-level AGI.

Because there are multiple routes to superintelligence, trying to slow down AI development by restricting just one area - like the computing power for training an AI model - won't be enough to stop overall progress. Equally, suppressing a single dimension risks creating a capability âoverhangâ: if multiple inputs need to be combined to make progress, holding back one dimension while the others move forward would lead to sudden, steep jumps in progress when the suppressed dimension is relaxed (or overcome otherwise).

Taking all these arguments together, continued fast AI progress over the next decade is a serious possibility. It could take us relatively smoothly from today, to Expert AGI, and then into the superhuman AI regime, accelerating science and enabling breakthroughs in fields like medicine, materials, and clean energy. Even in the absence of dramatic frontier AI progress, cognitive industrialization alone could reshape knowledge work and the broader economy. Regardless of which path AI progress takes, we must anticipate far-reaching opportunities along with equally transformative pressures to many aspects of human society.

It has been revealed that none of these predictions are certain, but the pathways and scenarios are also far from unfounded hype or fiction. So what can be done? Our best course of action may sound familiar: model, measure, forecast, and repeat. While those steps arenât surprising, the complexity and scale of carrying them out on the road to ASI is entirely unprecedented. It requires large-scale and highly-interdisciplinary efforts across both frontier labs and national and global institutions. Many of the key metrics for tracking progress on these pathways require frontier-model access and sizable amounts of evaluation compute, alongside latest benchmarking and modelling methodologies that could spawn entirely new research fields.

Recent findings suggest that human-level AGI has long been the horizon for AI research, but it is far from the upper limit of intelligence. Understanding what could come next - and its implications across science, industry, and society - is the grand challenge ahead for researchers, developers, and policymakers.

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

It has been revealed that not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a substantial "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be said for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

It has been revealed that because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before new models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

Price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

In a recent development, in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

The key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a new tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

It has been revealed that to avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

In a recent development, if you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

In a recent development, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

According to recent reports, yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

Sources indicate that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.
