💡 Key Takeaways
  • Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics.
  • According to recent reports, one of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality.
  • The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space.

According to recent reports, one of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

The basic idea of holographic duality is that some of these theoretical universes can be described in two ways: as a complete universe with gravity and spacetime, and in quantum terms, with no gravity at all, “written” on the universe’s outer boundary. Just as a real hologram encodes a 3D image on a 2D plane, the quantum model encodes all the information of the universe in one dimension fewer (a universe with four dimensions of space, for instance, can be fully described by a quantum theory with three). This lets physicists turn hard questions about gravity into questions about quantum physics, which are sometimes easier to answer.

According to recent reports, the first problem Claude solved concerns what happens when you heat up one of these theoretical universes. At low temperatures, the universe fills up with a gas of particles. Above a certain temperature, a black hole forms instead. In 1983, Stephen Hawking and Don Page highlighted that this switch is abrupt: it’s a phase transition, similar to how water suddenly boils at 100°C. But Hawking and Page’s calculation relies on general relativity, which holds only when the universe is vast, compared with the tiny scale at which that description breaks down. As the theoretical universe shrinks toward that smaller scale, spacetime loses any definite shape and becomes blurry, and nobody knows how to do the calculation on the gravity side of the duality. On the quantum side, though, the same situation can be calculated, at least in principle.

It has been revealed that in 1999, physicists found that there was a phase transition in that regime as well. But they didn’t know whether it was abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth. In 2003, a group of physicists set out the calculation that would settle the question, but it was extremely complex and was never completed. Claude did it by running a small research group of copies of itself, in which it worked out almost every piece of the calculation independently and checked its math against known results. It revealed that the phase transition is abrupt. The same sudden switch appears at both extremes, suggesting that black hole formation isn’t just a feature of relativity but is actually built into the underlying quantum theory.

The second problem concerns a simplified theoretical universe with two dimensions of space instead of three. This universe is straightforward enough to study in detail, but still has black holes and other mysteries similar to those of our own universe. Even in this simpler universe, physicists don’t know how to create a full theory of quantum gravity, so they approach it from the other direction: rather than building a single, correct theory, they try to rule out wrong ones by showing that they are internally inconsistent. This method is called bootstrapping.

Since 2009, physicists have used a version of this method to set a ceiling on how heavy the lightest black hole in such a universe could be. Any theory that breaks the ceiling is ruled out, and each lowering of the ceiling narrows the search. Results from numerical calculations hinted at where the best possible ceiling lay, but they couldn’t prove it, and the best proven ceiling was well short of what the numerical results suggested.

Claude Fable 5.2 noticed a pattern in the numerical results that physicists had missed and borrowed a method from elsewhere in math and physics to calculate the precise ceiling for the simplest version of this technique and prove that it could not be lowered. It doesn’t identify the correct theory, but it may point physicists in the right direction.

Neither result describes our own universe directly, and neither has practical applications, but both contribute to a long-running theoretical effort to understand how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together.

In the rest of this post, we explain in more detail what each problem was and what Claude did to solve them.

In a recent development, in August, an Anthropic researcher, Hongbin Chen, was testing Claude’s capabilities as a side project. He asked Claude to draw up a list of interesting open problems in theoretical physics, specifically focusing on black holes and the bootstrap method. Claude came back hours later with 22 candidates, and Hongbin set up separate agents to work on each one; they could read each other’s progress posts and collaborate when working on related problems. The agents ran in the background, with no special setup, for about six weeks.

Industry observers note that the agents solved the two problems in this post. One was the Hawking-Page phase transition, the question of when a hot gas turns into a black hole. Weeks after one of the agents reached a solution, a physicist, who had independently used Claude to tackle the same problem, shared his result, and a colleague realized that Hongbin’s agent had reached the same answer earlier. The two solutions used different methods, so they were a useful check on each other.

The modular bootstrap result came from several agents. The one that was assigned the problem spotted the pattern in the numerical results when surveying the bootstrap literature, and another one—which was working on a mathematically related problem about how tightly spheres can be packed into a high-dimensional space—turned that pattern into a method. It found that this method reproduced a sphere-packing result recently proved by an OpenAI model. Claude then applied the same method to the bootstrap problem, which an earlier Claude agent had tried, and failed, to solve in 61 parallel attempts. Two other agents also independently arrived at the same answer. One half of the final proof, showing that the ceiling can’t be lowered, follows the strategy of the OpenAI proof. In September, the results were formally verified in Lean, a computerized proof checker. Claude then wrote the paper with minimal guidance, and a physicist checked every main result.

To understand the first problem, we need to start with something much more familiar: a walk through Newly introduced York City.

Imagine that you’re heading from Penn Station to the High Line entrance on West 30th Street and 10th Avenue, and there are two equally good routes. You could walk west along West 33rd Street and turn south, or head south first and then walk west along West 30th Street. Either way, you have to pick one. In the quantum world, though, that’s not true: a particle can take both routes simultaneously.

This is most clearly demonstrated in the famous double-slit experiment. In this test, you fire particles, one at a time, at a barrier cut with two narrow slits, and record where, on a screen behind it, each one lands. Each particle lands at a particular point on the screen, as a particle should. But as you fire more of them, they build up a pattern of stripes that would only be possible if each one had passed through both slits, like a wave.

To predict what a quantum particle will do more generally, physicists have to add up every path it could possibly take, known as its possible histories. Not every history counts equally; some contribute far more to the sum than others. It’s an extravagant and mysterious way to describe how a single particle behaves, but it’s also one of the most successful ideas in physics.

Industry observers note that this approach, known as the “sum over histories,” is well established for particles and anything made of them. But what about gravity? Einstein highlighted that gravity is a consequence of curved spacetime: objects with mass bend space and time around them, and we feel that bending as gravity. In a quantum theory of gravity, therefore, what gets summed over is the shape of spacetime itself, rather than just the paths of particles moving through it. To make predictions in a quantum theory of gravity, we would have to add up every shape that the universe could possibly take, and nobody yet knows how to do that. Much of modern quantum gravity research is an attempt to work it out.

Recent findings suggest that hawking and Page found a case where this sum is simple enough to handle but still interesting. To explain Hawking and Page’s work, we need to imagine a different kind of universe, called anti-de Sitter spacetime. Imagine you’re standing in a giant bowl. No matter how hard you throw an object, it will always roll back to the place you threw it from.

Our universe isn’t like that. The difference comes down to a quantity called the cosmological constant, which describes the energy of empty space. In our universe, this energy is positive, which makes space expand ever faster. In anti-de Sitter spacetime, the energy is negative, so everything is pulled back to where it started. Hawking and Page chose this universe for their calculation because of how it behaves when it heats up: the bowl keeps heat in so it can stay at a steady temperature.

At any given temperature, two histories matter far more than all the others. Here, a “history” means an entire version of the universe: a particular shape of spacetime, along with everything in it. In one, the bowl is filled with an ordinary gas of particles—including gravitons, the particles believed to carry gravity. In the other, it contains a black hole. Whichever contributes more to the sum is, in effect, what we would observe—it “wins.” At low temperatures, the gas history wins, and the universe is full of gas; at high temperatures, the black-hole history wins, and the universe contains a black hole. At one particular temperature—which physicists now call the Hawking-Page temperature—the universe switches abruptly from one to the other. This is the phase transition.

It’s a rare case where we can see two very different shapes of spacetime competing in the sum over histories, and can say which one wins.

This is where the holographic principle enters the story. In the 1970s, Jacob Bekenstein and Hawking found that the amount of information a black hole can hold is proportional to its surface area, not to its volume. That’s very different from ordinary matter, where every bit of volume holds roughly the same amount of information.

In a recent development, in the early 1990s, Gerard ’t Hooft and Leonard Susskind proposed that this idea applies to gravity in general—that everything inside a region of space can be fully described by the information on its boundary, just as a flat hologram can display a three-dimensional image. In 1997, Juan Maldacena formalized the idea further. Gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl, he argued, is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory of particles, with no gravity at all, existing on the rim of the bowl (the universe’s outer boundary). These are the gravity side and the quantum side of the duality we described in the introduction—they’re two languages for describing the same underlying reality.

In the case Claude studied, the quantum theory on the rim is called N=4 super Yang-Mills theory. It’s related to the theories that describe how particles interact in the real universe, but it has extra symmetries that make it much easier for physicists to work with. (Claude has worked with this theory before, calculating how particles interact within it to a new level of precision.) Since the gravity side predicts two histories competing with each other, the obvious question is: does N=4 super Yang-Mills theory (the quantum side) show the same thing?

It has been revealed that for now, physicists can analyze this theory in detail only when its particles barely interact with each other, a condition known as weak coupling. This is the opposite end of the spectrum from where Hawking and Page’s gravitational calculation works. Weak coupling on the quantum side corresponds to the small, blurry universe on the gravity side. So there was no guarantee that any of Hawking and Page’s findings would hold there.

It has been revealed that remarkably, they do. Bo Sundborg in 1999, and after him Ofer Aharony, Joseph Marsano, Shiraz Minwalla, Kyriakos Papadodimas, and Mark Van Raamsdonk, revealed that even at weak coupling, the theory on the rim goes through a transition as it heats up. This is its counterpart of the switch from gas to black hole inside the bowl. But it was still unknown whether this transition is abrupt, like Hawking and Page’s, or smooth and gradual.

Sources indicate that when particles barely interact, physicists have to calculate how they behave one step at a time. They start with a simplified version of the theory in which particles don’t interact at all. Then they add a series of corrections, each more precise and harder to compute than the last. Physicists call these steps loops. In 2003, Aharony and his colleagues realized that whether the phase transition was an abrupt jump, as Hawking and Page predicted, or gradual, hinged on a single number that appeared only three loops in. Computing that number involves many thousands of terms, known as diagrams—far too many to work through by hand. In 2005, the same group completed the calculation for a simpler cousin of the theory and found an abrupt transition. But the version for N=4 super Yang-Mills, more than 10 times larger, was never completed.

The scale of the computational problem, while daunting, wasn’t the only obstacle to completing the calculation. There was a conceptual glitch, as well: naively adding up all the parts of the calculation gives an infinite answer, and those infinities have to be tamed carefully to extract a meaningful result.

According to recent reports, to solve the problem, Claude ran a small research group of agents, all copies of itself. Almost every piece of the calculation was done twice, by agents acting independently. For extra consistency checks, parts of the calculation could also be compared to previous results in the literature.

According to recent reports, the result Claude found is an abrupt jump as the temperature rises, exactly analogous to what Hawking and Page had found using the sum over spacetime histories. The emerging picture is very simple: the transition is abrupt at both weak and strong coupling—the blurry and the smooth ends, in the gravity description. The most natural possibility is that it stays abrupt everywhere in between.

This is a beautiful outcome. It highlights that a calculation using the sum over histories in gravity qualitatively matches the behavior of an ordinary quantum theory with no gravity at all.

Industry observers note that many open questions remain. The abrupt transition Claude found is very much like the one we see whenever we boil water. One interesting feature of abrupt transitions is that the losing side of the competition can survive for a while: for instance, water can be superheated above 100°C without boiling, as you could see for yourself if you were to put a cup of extremely pure water in the microwave. (But please don’t do this; it’s dangerous, and Anthropic would rather not be responsible for an epidemic of scalded readers.).

Something similar happens here. Above the Hawking-Page temperature, the hot gas of gravitons and other particles can survive for a long time in a superheated state. But at a higher temperature it can no longer survive: this is another transition, the Hagedorn transition, which is a characteristic signature of string theory. On the gravity side, that transition has many interesting properties of its own, and it would be valuable to check in detail whether they also appear in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Industry observers note that another open question concerns the other possible histories of spacetime. Hawking and Page considered three: one in which their model universe is filled with gas, one that contains a large black hole, and one containing a smaller black hole that never comes to dominate the sum over histories. In principle, there are many more possible histories. As far as anyone knows, none of them ever dominates. But given certain changes to the starting conditions—if the universe is set spinning, for instance, or given a fixed amount of energy or charge—then some of these histories do take over. Working out exactly which ones win, and when, is an interesting problem for the future.

Recent findings suggest that as we saw earlier, one useful model universe has just two dimensions of space and one of time: it’s called “3D gravity” because it describes gravity in three spacetime dimensions. According to the principle of holographic duality, 3D gravity inside the anti-de Sitter bowl is equivalent to an ordinary quantum theory living on the bowl’s rim.

As a model, 3D gravity is much simpler than the real thing, but it still allows for black holes and many of the same mysteries. It provides a useful laboratory for studying the sum over spacetime histories. It’s also a good place to test the idea that spacetime isn’t a basic ingredient of the universe, but emerges from something deeper. In general relativity, black holes look smooth. But in quantum gravity, if you zoom in to the smallest scales—the Planck length, around 10-35 meters, where quantum effects on gravity become impossible to ignore—black holes are made of an enormous number of tiny, individual building blocks. Physicists believe the same is true in our own, four-dimensional universe, but the 3D version is much easier to analyze with holographic duality.

Claude’s results build on a method called the bootstrap, a general strategy for solving quantum theories. Counterintuitively, the strategy doesn’t try to solve a theory directly. For 3D gravity, that isn’t even possible, because nobody knows how to define the theory precisely. Instead, the bootstrap rules theories out by showing that they contradict themselves. Physicists scan over all possible quantum theories and try to eliminate them one by one.

In a recent development, remarkably, in many cases this method makes it possible to pinpoint a single quantum theory and calculate precisely how it behaves. The requirements of relativity and quantum mechanics are so demanding, and so delicately balanced, that together they rule out every alternative. In 2012, the bootstrap was used to solve a quantum field theory called the 3D critical Ising model, a simple model of magnetism that also describes water at the point where liquid and vapor become indistinguishable. Since then, it has been applied to many different quantum systems.

In 2009, Simeon Hellerman introduced a technique called the modular bootstrap, which applies the bootstrap method to 3D gravity. Its goal is to rule out inconsistent theories of quantum gravity in three spacetime dimensions. By combining it with other bootstrap methods, physicists hope to eventually eliminate every inconsistent theory. Whatever is left must be consistent. There could be no consistent theories, or just one, or whole families of them. Any of these outcomes would be interesting, because it would help us understand what spacetime looks like at the Planck scale in this simplified universe, and give us hints about the Planck scale in our own.

Here’s how the modular bootstrap works. 3D gravity in anti-de Sitter spacetime has a quantity called the central charge (c), which roughly counts how many microscopic building blocks the universe is made of. When general relativity holds, c is very large, because large black holes contain an enormous number of building blocks. A second quantity, M₁, is the mass of the lightest black hole. To run the bootstrap, physicists scan over every possible theory, with every possible value of c and M₁, and look for inconsistencies.

Recent findings suggest that to understand how that search works, we need to go back to the sum over spacetime histories. In 3D gravity, that means adding up different 3D shapes of spacetime. They can be simple, like a ball, or more complicated, like the donut and two-holed donut in the figure below. The spacetime is the inside of the shape—the dough inside the donut. Its surface, like the rim of the bowl in the earlier section, is where the quantum theory is “written,” in one fewer dimension.

Sources indicate that the modular bootstrap starts with a spacetime shaped like an ordinary, one-holed donut, or torus. There are two different ways to interpret this shape, depending on which direction we call “time” and which we call “space.” In the first, the long direction around the hole is time and the other, shorter loop, around the tube, is space. In the second, they’re swapped: the long loop is space and the shorter loop is time.

In a recent development, in calculations like these, the length of the time loop sets the temperature: the shorter the loop, the hotter the universe. So swapping the two loops trades a cold universe for a hot one. The two interpretations correspond to the two competing histories that Hawking and Page studied. In 3D gravity there are no gravitons, but there is a transition similar to the one that Claude analyzed in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory.

Now we come to the crucial step. In relativity, space and time are on an equal footing. So it can’t matter which loop we label space and which we label time. As far as relativity is concerned, the two interpretations are equivalent, and the physics must be the same for every possible experiment.

Quantum mechanics, however, treats time differently from space. To calculate anything, you pick a direction to call time and track how the system evolves along it. So, when we calculate observable quantities in quantum gravity, the two interpretations of the donut lead to calculations that look very different. But in relativity, it doesn’t matter which loop is called time, so the two calculations have to give exactly the same answer.

According to recent reports, if we knew the theory of 3D quantum gravity, we could do both calculations and confirm that they match. We don’t, but with the bootstrap method, that isn’t a problem. Physicists scan over the possible values of c (the number of building blocks) and M₁ (the mass of the lightest black hole). For each pair of values, they try to prove that the theory would be inconsistent—that the two calculations on the donut couldn’t possibly give the same answer. This involves searching for a special mathematical object called a bootstrap functional. If physicists find one, then the theory is inconsistent, and those values are ruled out.

The hope, supported by the bootstrap’s successes elsewhere, is that combining this approach with other bootstrap methods will eventually rule out most possible theories of 3D quantum gravity. The theories left standing would be the only ones consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics. Physicists could then use them to explore some of the biggest questions in quantum gravity: is there only one theory? Does it rely on string theory, or are there alternatives? What are black holes made of at the microscopic level, and how do we sum over spacetime histories?

This strategy can work in principle, but it’s very difficult in practice, because bootstrap functionals are hard to find. What matters for quantum gravity is what happens when c is large—but the larger c gets, the harder the search becomes. In the original paper on the modular bootstrap, Hellerman proved that in any consistent theory of 3D gravity, M₁ can be no larger than c/6, up to small corrections. Theories with a heavier lightest black hole can’t possibly be consistent with both gravity and quantum mechanics.

In a recent development, the goal of the modular bootstrap is to push this ceiling as low as possible, pinning down how heavy the lightest black hole can be. Physicists write the ceiling as M₁ ≤ c/Λ. A lower ceiling means a larger number Λ. The results below, including Claude’s, concern the simplest and most-studied version of the method, which ignores how the black holes spin.

In a recent development, over the past 15 years, physicists have worked to lower the ceiling and pin down the theory as tightly as possible. There are two ways to do this. One is analytical—building a bootstrap functional by hand, with pen-and-paper mathematics. The other is numerical—using computers to search for functionals and optimize them. The results of these numerical calculations suggested that the modular bootstrap could push the ceiling down to about c/9.1. But these calculations get harder as c grows, so they couldn’t settle the question. On the analytical side, Tom Hartman, Dalimil Mazáč, and Leonardo Rastelli proved a ceiling of c/8.5, but because this was higher than the numerical results had suggested, this clearly wasn’t the best the modular bootstrap could do. Since then, just how tightly the modular bootstrap can constrain quantum gravity has remained an open question.

It has been revealed that claude set about solving the problem by running numerical experiments and reproducing results from the literature. In doing so, it noticed a pattern that physicists had so far missed, involving the way the numerical ceiling shifted slightly as c grew. Based on that pattern, Claude developed a hypothesis about the behavior of the bootstrap functional, using a mathematical tool called a spectral curve. Spectral curves are well known in other areas of mathematics and physics, but had never been applied to this problem. Claude found the spectral curve that governs the modular bootstrap at large values of c. It then used it to prove that the lightest black hole in 3D quantum gravity can be no heavier than c/Λ, where Λ is given by an exact formula and is approximately 9.1266. It also proved that this ceiling is optimal: it’s the lowest this version of the modular bootstrap can ever go. Claude delivered the solution across four research notes, which it later merged into a single paper.

This is one of the first times the bootstrap has been used to derive an exact result in the regime of quantum gravity where black holes matter. It also shows that this version of the method can’t, on its own, push the ceiling down to c/12, the mass at which black holes first appear; that will take other ingredients. Although it doesn’t pin down the theory of quantum gravity in three dimensions by itself, it provides a starting point and helps to narrow the search.

These two results show Claude doing two very different kinds of research. The first is a known calculation that physicists had set aside for two decades, because the work was too long and error-prone to complete by hand. The second required a latest idea: spotting a pattern others had missed and bringing in a mathematical tool from another area of physics. Both were carried out largely autonomously. Neither result settles the question of quantum gravity, or even comes close to doing so, but each pushes physics forward in a longstanding area of research.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences.
  • In a recent development, what eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers.
  • Heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences. As someone who is easily squeamish, I’ll admit that when I first tuned in years ago, I almost abandoned the show altogether, too disturbed by watching teenagers hunt their friends like animals and decapitate corpses to continue.

In a recent development, what eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers. Adding to that was “Yellowjackets’” knack for unveiling mysteries that left viewers, myself included, desperate for answers.

Heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords. The major questions that kept audiences hooked for years now demand answers before the series finale. Likewise, the interwoven narrative — jumping between the teenage plane crash survivors stranded in the wilderness and their adult counterparts — has always been an effective tool, but before the end, these timelines need to find a satisfying cohesion.

Having watched the first eight of season 4's 10 episodes, I can safely and somewhat unfortunately say that while “Yellowjackets” satisfies in some areas, it falls short in others — and it doesn’t have much time left to course-correct.

Sources indicate that easily the most compelling aspect of these first eight episodes is the exploration of the team’s return home. For three seasons, audiences knew these traumatized kids — the ones who survived, at least — would eventually make it back, with the adult timeline confirming several names (Shauna, Misty, and Melissa among them).

It has been revealed that prior to season 4, however, “Yellowjackets” had yet to reveal that exact moment of return and its immediate fallout: watching characters who hunted, killed, and ate their friends attempt to slip back into their “normal” lives. While the adult timeline already proved the survivors never truly moved past their ordeal, seeing their parent reunions, the jarring shift in high school social dynamics, and the strange fame that comes with surviving a mass tragedy is precisely what audiences have been waiting for.

With just two episodes to go, a shocking number of questions remain on the table, raising an obvious concern: has “Yellowjackets” saved too much for an epic finale? Of the many shows met with controversy over their endings, the mind-bending sci-fi series “Lost” is among the most notorious and perhaps the closest comparison to “Yellowjackets” in its approach to mystery and suspense.

Industry observers note that like “Lost,” “Yellowjackets” has spent years building complex mysteries whose reveals appear to be crammed into the final two episodes. In the case of “Lost,” that famously backfired, leaving even dedicated fans frustrated by how questions were answered, the breakneck speed with which some were “resolved,” or the fact that certain mysteries went unaddressed forever.

Sources indicate that based on episodes 1 through 8, “Yellowjackets” season 4 seems to be heading down a very similar path. Several of the show’s most captivating questions haven't just gone unanswered by the end of episode 8, they’ve been largely ignored. Hopefully, this doesn't mean answers are never coming, which would undoubtedly trigger a wave of backlash akin to “Lost.” Even if the finale delivers, it would have been far more satisfying to see this final season deeply flesh out the truth of the wilderness — whether it’s a supernatural force or simply a manifestation of the survivors’ trauma — well before the final curtain.

Ultimately, “Yellowjackets” Season 4 is an exciting final entry that showcases the cast at the top of their game and finally gives audiences a real look at how the survivors reacclimated—or failed to—after nearly two years in the wild. Still, for the final chapter of a show that has captivated viewers for five years, the series has left itself too much ground to cover in too little time.

Industry observers note that while heavy narrative exposition was always inevitable in Season 4—especially with so much left unresolved in the adult timeline—what audiences really want heading into the finale are answers, not more questions. With the clock very much ticking, “Yellowjackets” still has to prove it can stick the landing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A smartphone displaying the Google search start screen.

In a recent development, google Quantum AI says it has shown contextuality, a quantum property thought to power some algorithms, on up to 105 qubits, in a paper on the cover of Science. The tests also expose subtle hardware errors, but the paper does not claim an unconditional advantage over classical computers.

In a recent development, google Quantum AI indicates a quantum property thought to power some algorithms still holds on up to 105 qubits. The research, published on Thursday on the cover of Science, tested the property on Google’s superconducting quantum processors.

According to recent reports, the property is called contextuality. It means a measurement’s result is not fixed in advance, but depends on which other measurements are made alongside it. Until now, it had mostly been shown in systems of just a few particles.

In one test, Google’s qubits won a two-player game, the Mermin-Peres magic square, 98.3% of the time. The best possible classical strategy wins only 88.9% of the time. A larger task using 105 qubits also beat classical strategies with limited resources.

Industry observers note that google states the tests double as a sensitive way to catch subtle hardware errors that other benchmarks miss. It says this could help pave the way for uses in chemistry and materials science, though the experiments did not simulate either.

The paper is careful about its limits. It claims there is no unconditional proof that quantum computers beat classical ones in general, and its quantum edge in one game shrank as more qubits joined. The work first appeared as a preprint in December 2025.

Industry observers note that error-free hardware remains the industry’s big goal. Google has said it wants a useful, error-corrected quantum computer by 2029, and Microsoft, which unveiled its Majorana 2 chip in June, has set the same target.

Industry observers note that IBM agreed to buy HRL as it demonstrated a chip that corrects its own errors, and Nvidia has simulated a 104-qubit error-corrected machine. Investors are piling in too, with Quantinuum raising $1.68B in its IPO in June.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

In a recent development, this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

PostgreSQL 19

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Postgresql

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including:.
  • According to recent reports, latest REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance.
  • pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies strategy advice automatically based on the query.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including:.

According to recent reports, latest REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table.

pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies strategy advice automatically based on the query.

Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations.

Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica.

Logical replication of sequence values.

Support for “read-your-writes” consistency on standbys via the newly introduced WAIT command.

Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a newly introduced scoring system.

The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below.

Sources indicate that A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to latest major releases.

Sources indicate that version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities:.

Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) §.

The default warning period is seven days.

Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) §.

The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings. MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18.

Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) §.

PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP, which is unfixably insecure.

Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) §.

Sources indicate that dumps created using pre-PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall, and using standard_conforming_strings = off, will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. People should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on.

In a recent development, client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off, for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary.

Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) §.

It has been revealed that pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems.

Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § §.

It has been revealed that the btree_gist inet/cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet/cidr indexes.

Industry observers note that disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) §.

The values of such columns were not well-defined.

Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) §.

Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) §.

This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions.

Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) §.

Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases.

Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) §.

This has been replaced by four newly introduced variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2.

Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) §.

In a recent development, previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT.

Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) §.

According to recent reports, previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit. With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases.

Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) §.

This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately.

Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) §.

Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared, BufferShareExclusive, and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) §.

Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) §.

Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) §.

Change psql's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) §.

Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) §.

Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU, builtin) and where the locale configured through that locale provider behaves differently from the LC_CTYPE setting configured for the database, particularly a LC_CTYPE of C, the output of some full text search and pg_trgm functions could change. When upgrading such databases using pg_upgrade, it is recommended to reindex all indexes which use full text search and pg_trgm after the upgrade, and to recompute any stored tsvector values.

Change how fuzzystrmatch functions handle non-ASCII characters (Peter Eisentraut, Jeff Davis) § §.

dmetaphone() and dmetaphone_alt() now upper-case their input using the database's default collation rather than always using libc, and soundex(), metaphone(), and difference() now treat only ASCII letters as letters. When upgrading with pg_upgrade, it is recommended to reindex any indexes that use these functions after the upgrade.

Remove MULE_INTERNAL encoding (Thomas Munro) §.

It has been revealed that this encoding was complex and rarely used. Databases using it will need to be dumped and restored with a different encoding.

Below you will find a detailed account of the changes between PostgreSQL 19 and the previous major release.

Allow NOT IN clauses to be converted to more efficient ANTI JOINs when NULLs are not present (Richard Guo) §.

Allow more LEFT JOINs to be converted to ANTI JOINs (Tender Wang, Richard Guo) §.

Allow use of Memoize for ANTI JOINs with unique inner sides (Richard Guo) §.

Allow some aggregate processing to be performed before joins (Richard Guo, Antonin Houska) § § §.

This can reduce the number of rows needed to be processed.

Improve hash join's handling of tuples with NULL join keys (Tom Lane) §.

Improve the planning of semijoins (Richard Guo) §.

Allow Append and MergeAppend to consider explicit incremental sorts (Richard Guo) §.

Convert IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM NULL to IS [NOT] NULL during constant folding (Richard Guo) §.

The latter form is more easily optimized.

Simplify IS [NOT] DISTINCT FROM to equality/inequality operators when inputs are proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) §.

Perform earlier constant folding of var IS [NOT] NULL in the optimizer (Richard Guo) §.

This allows for later optimizations.

Simplify COALESCE() and ROW(...) IS [NOT] NULL to avoid evaluating unnecessary arguments (Richard Guo) § §.

Simplify IS [NOT] TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN to plain boolean expressions when the input is proven non-nullable (Richard Guo) §.

Speed up join selectivity computations for large optimizer statistics targets (Ilia Evdokimov, David Geier) §.

Add proper optimizer statistics for functions returning boolean values (Tom Lane) §.

Allow extended statistics on virtual generated columns (Yugo Nagata) §.

Allow function pg_restore_extended_stats() to restore optimizer extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier, Chao Li) § § § §.

Add function pg_clear_extended_stats() to remove extended statistics (Corey Huinker, Michael Paquier) §.

Adjust the optimizer to consider startup costs of partial paths (Robert Haas, Tomas Vondra) §.

Allow negative values of pg_aggregate.aggtransspace to indicate unbounded memory usage (Richard Guo) §.

This information is used by the optimizer in planning memory usage.

Improve performance of foreign key constraint checks (Junwang Zhao, Amit Langote, Chao Li) § §.

Improve asynchronous I/O read-ahead scheduling for large requests (Andres Freund) § § §.

Allow io_method method worker to automatically control needed background workers (Thomas Munro) §.

The latest server variables are io_min_workers, io_max_workers, io_worker_idle_timeout, and io_worker_launch_interval.

Allow query table scans to mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map (Melanie Plageman) §.

It has been revealed that previously only VACUUM and COPY ... FREEZE could do this.

Allow autovacuum to use parallel autovacuum workers (Daniil Davydov) § §.

The maximum number of workers is controlled by server variable autovacuum_max_parallel_workers and per-table storage parameter autovacuum_parallel_workers.

Allow TID Range Scans to be parallelized (Cary Huang, David Rowley) §.

Improve COPY FROM performance for text and CSV input using SIMD CPU instructions (Nazir Bilal Yavuz, Shinya Kato) §.

Improve NOTIFY to only wake up backends that are listening to specified notifications (Joel Jacobson) §.

Previously most backends were woken by NOTIFY.

Change wal_compression equals on to use the best WAL compression method available (wenhui qiu) §.

Previously this always used pglz.

Change the default TOAST compression method from pglz to the more efficient lz4 (Euler Taveira) §.

This is done by changing the default for server variable default_toast_compression.

Improve performance of internal row deformation (David Rowley) §.

Improve performance of repeated UTF-8 case-folding operations (Andreas Karlsson) §.

Improve performance of hash index bulk-deletion and GIN index vacuuming using streaming reads (Xuneng Zhou) § §.

Improve sort performance using radix sort (John Naylor) §.

Improve timing performance measurements (Lukas Fittl, Andres Freund, David Geier) § §.

This benefits EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, TIMING) and pg_test_timing, and is controlled via server variable timing_clock_source.

Optimize plpgsql syntax SELECT simple-expression INTO var (Tom Lane) §.

Add system view pg_stat_lock and function pg_stat_get_lock() to report per-lock-type statistics (Bertrand Drouvot) §.

Add system view pg_stat_recovery to report recovery status (Xuneng Zhou, Shinya Kato) § §.

Add system view pg_stat_progress_repack to report the progress of REPACK, CLUSTER, and VACUUM FULL (Álvaro Herrera) §.

Add system view pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to report per-table autovacuum details (Sami Imseih) §.

Add vacuum initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_vacuum (Shinya Kato) §.

The new started_by column reports the initiator of the vacuum, and mode indicates its aggressiveness.

Add analyze initiation details to system view pg_stat_progress_analyze (Shinya Kato) §.

The new started_by column reports the initiator of the analyze.

Add system view pg_dsm_registry_allocations to report dynamic shared memory details (Florents Tselai, Nathan Bossart) § §.

Add mem_exceeded_count column to system view pg_stat_replication_slots (Bertrand Drouvot) §.

The new columns are slotsync_skip_count, slotsync_last_skip, and slotsync_skip_reason.

Add backup_type column to system view pg_stat_progress_basebackup to report the type of backup (Shinya Kato) §.

Possible values are full or incremental.

Adds table OID and attribute number columns to pg_stats, and table OID and statistics object OID columns to the other two.

The fresh format is type:level. A value without a colon controls all process types, allowing backward compatibility.

This is also enabled when the server is started with debug level three and higher.

These include replication, postgres_fdw, and dblink servers.

Have pg_get_sequence_data() return the sequence page LSN (Vignesh C) §.

Add function pg_get_multixact_stats() to report multixact activity (Naga Appani) §.

Issue warnings when the wraparound of transaction IDs or multixacts is less than 100 million away (Nathan Bossart) §.

In a recent development, the previous warning was 40 million. Warnings are issued to clients and in the server log.

The new server variables are autovacuum_freeze_score_weight, autovacuum_multixact_freeze_score_weight, autovacuum_vacuum_score_weight, autovacuum_vacuum_insert_score_weight, and autovacuum_analyze_score_weight.

New configuration file PGDATA/pg_hosts.conf specifies hostname/key pairs.

Allow roles pg_read_all_data and pg_write_all_data to read/write large objects (Nitin Motiani, Nathan Bossart) §.

These roles are designed to allow non-super users to run pg_dump.

Allow background workers to be configured to terminate before database-level operations (Aya Iwata) §.

This allows database-level operations to complete more promptly since blocking background workers can now be terminated.

Patch GB18030 encoding from version 2000 to 2022 (Chao Li, Zheng Tao) §.

See the commit message for compatibility details.

Improve function pg_sync_replication_slots() to wait for replication synchronization completion (Ajin Cherian, Zhijie Hou) §.

Previously, certain synchronization failures would not be reported.

By default, senders still wait forever for synchronization.

This occurs during ALTER SUBSCRIPTION ... [ADD|SET|REFRESH|DROP] PUBLICATION. Function pg_get_sequence_data() allows inspection of sequence synchronization.

This is enabled with the ALL SEQUENCES clause.

This is enabled with the REFRESH SEQUENCES clause.

Allow CREATE/ALTER PUBLICATION to exclude some tables (Vignesh C, Shlok Kyal) § § § §.

This is controlled with the EXCEPT clause, and is useful when specifying ALL TABLES.

Add CREATE/ALTER SUBSCRIPTION setting retain_dead_tuples to retain information needed for conflict detection (Zhijie Hou) § § §.

Allow CREATE SUBSCRIPTION to use postgres_fdw foreign data wrapper connection parameters (Jeff Davis) §.

The connection parameters are referenced via CREATE SUBSCRIPTION ... SERVER.

Allow wal_receiver_timeout to be set per-subscription and user (Fujii Masao) § §.

Allow GROUP BY to process target list subqueries that have expressions referencing non-subquery columns (Tom Lane) §.

Add support for INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT ... RETURNING (Andreas Karlsson, Marko Tiikkaja, Viktor Holmberg) §.

This allows conflicting rows to be returned, and optionally locked with FOR UPGRADE/SHARE.

Add REPACK command which replaces VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER (Antonin Houska) §.

According to recent reports, the two former commands did similar things, but with confusing names, so unify them as REPACK. The old commands have been retained for compatibility.

Allow REPACK to rebuild tables without access-exclusive locking (Antonin Houska, Mihail Nikalayeu, Álvaro Herrera) § § §.

Allow GRANT/REVOKE to specify the effective role performing the privileges adjustment (Nathan Bossart, Tom Lane) §.

The GRANTED BY clause controls this.

Previously enforcement changes were only supported for foreign key constraints.

This was previously prohibited.

Previously only a single header line could be skipped.

Allow COPY FROM to set invalid input values to NULL (Jian He, Kirill Reshke) §.

JSON output can also be a single JSON array using the COPY option FORCE_ARRAY.

Allow COPY TO to process partitioned tables (Jian He, Ajin Cherian) § §.

Previously COPY (SELECT ...) had to be used to output partitioned tables. This also improves logical replication table synchronization.

This can show why Memoize was chosen.

Add the 64-bit unsigned data type oid8 (Michael Paquier) §.

Industry observers note that add more jsonpath string methods (Florents Tselai, David E. Wheeler) §.

It has been revealed that they are ltrim(), rtrim(), btrim(), lower(), upper(), initcap(), replace(), and split_part(). These are immutable like their non-JSON string variants.

Allow casts between bytea and uuid data types (Dagfinn Ilmari Mannsåker, Aleksander Alekseev) §.

Add ability to cast between database names and oids using regdatabase (Ian Lawrence Barwick) §.

Add date, timestamp, and timestamptz versions of random(min, max) (Damien Clochard, Dean Rasheed) § §.

Allow encode() and decode() to process data in base64url and base32hex formats (Andrey Borodin, Aleksander Alekseev, Florents Tselai) § § §.

This format retains ordering, unlike base32.

Add functions to return a set of ranges resulting from range subtraction (Paul A. Jungwirth) §.

The functions are range_minus_multi() and multirange_minus_multi(). This is useful to represent range subtraction results with gaps.

Add function error_on_null() to return the supplied parameter, or error on NULL input (Joel Jacobson) §.

Allow IS JSON to work on domains defined over supported base types (Jian He) §.

The supported base types are TEXT, JSON, JSONB, and BYTEA.

The Dutch stemmer now uses a different algorithm, which changes the stems of many words; the previous algorithm is available via dutch_porter.

The English, French, German, Lithuanian, Norwegian, Spanish, Swedish, and Turkish stemmers have also been updated and produce different stems for some words.

Allow event triggers to be written using PL/Python (Euler Taveira, Dimitri Fontaine) §.

Otherwise known as protocol grease, which was active during the 19 beta period. These will no longer be sent as of the PostgreSQL 19 official release, but the parameter reservations will remain for potential use in the future.

The UNSAFE option still generates all debugging output.

This works when psql is connected to PostgreSQL 18 or later.

The modified commands are \dRp+, \dRs+, and \dX+.

The \pset variables are display_true and display_false.

Allow psql to more accurately determine if the pager is needed (Erik Wienhold) §.

Add or improve psql tab completion (Yamaguchi Atsuo, Yugo Nagata, Haruna Miwa, Xuneng Zhou, Dagfinn Ilmari Mannsåker, Fujii Masao, Álvaro Herrera, Jian He, Tatsuya Kawata, Ian Lawrence Barwick, Vasuki M) § § § § § § § § § § § § § §.

Allow pg_dump to include restorable extended statistics (Corey Huinker) §.

Latest Update: Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, noted last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

Industry observers note that in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

#3908. Running iOS 27 on an older iPhone? These 3 non-AI upgrades actually improve how you use it every day

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomsguide ↗ Open Full Page

Running iOS 27 on an older iPhone? These 3 non-AI upgrades actually improve how you use it every day

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions.
  • If you have been putting off the enhancement assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering.
  • Scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions. The catch is that Apple Intelligence requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, leaving anyone holding onto an older compatible handset locked out of the headline feature.

If you have been putting off the enhancement assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering. Beneath the AI marketing, Apple rolled out several high-impact security, camera, and interface upgrades that run without Apple Intelligence — and these three additions make a meaningful difference in daily use.

Scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials. Introduced in iOS 27, Impersonation Risk Detection serves as Apple’s built-in defense against this social engineering, and it works without requiring Apple Intelligence.

To activate it, open Settings, tap Privacy & Security, scroll down and select Impersonation Risk Detection, then toggle it on.

It has been revealed that the system monitors on-device interaction patterns and behavioral cues during high-stakes actions without reading your personal messages, emails, or photos. If you attempt a large transfer or sensitive account change under signs of coercion, your iPhone flags the event and directs supported banking apps to require secondary verification before funds can leave your account.

Over the last few iOS updates, Apple has tucked more manual toggles behind the Camera app’s six-dot menu, adding extra taps whenever you want to tweak exposure, aspect ratio, or timer settings before taking a shot. iOS 27 fixes that friction by letting you pin your essential controls directly to the top of the viewfinder.

Recent findings suggest that launch the Camera app, tap the six-dot icon and hit Edit in the top-left corner. From there, tap any highlighted tools you want kept within thumb’s reach, remove shortcuts you rarely touch using the minus badge, and tap Done.

Even better, iOS 27 saves separate pinned layouts per shooting mode, allowing you to tailor your quick-access toolbar individually for Photo, Portrait, Video, Cinematic, Slow-Mo, and Time-Lapse.

Apple’s translucent Liquid Glass design has remained one of iOS’s most polarizing visual shifts since its debut, particularly when semi-transparent menus sit over bright or busy wallpapers. Rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all look, iOS 27 introduces a dedicated precision slider so you can tailor how much transparency appears across your system interface.

  • Industry observers note that JPMorgan Chase states hackers got into data held by companies that work for the bank, and that it may include some customers’ names and email addresses.
  • We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.
  • Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that JPMorgan Chase states hackers got into data held by companies that work for the bank, and that it may include some customers’ names and email addresses. Visa and Mastercard have also confirmed incidents at outside providers.

We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack.

Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.

There is no disruption to our services.

Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring.

There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week.

— Chase (@Chase) November 19, 2026.

The bank said the attackers accessed marketing data held by those vendors. Its own services kept running. It will offer affected customers free credit monitoring where appropriate.

Chase also noted the attack has no link to Monday’s outage, which it blamed on a software bug in its own hardware.

A ransomware gang called n0n published the data after a 48-hour deadline passed, Cybernews reported. Its researchers found about 16,000 customer email addresses, Chase account IDs and, in some cases, phone numbers. The file also holds 124 email addresses of bank staff.

All of the records seem to relate to Chase’s Reserve card, Cybernews remarked. The invitation-only Visa card is for wealthy clients, usually with at least $10m in managed assets.

“This association alone makes the leak a lot more sensitive,” said Aras Nazarovas, a senior security researcher at Cybernews.

The file is only 502KB. It is not clear whether it is a sample or all the gang took. TNW has not independently verified the data.

In a recent development, A Mastercard spokesperson told Business Insider that an outside provider exposed a limited number of email addresses. They belong to a small group of cardholders in one benefit programme. Mastercard said it has contained the exposure.

“There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards,” the spokesperson remarked.

Visa said its incident involved a service provider in the Asia Pacific region.

“Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected,” a Visa spokesperson remarked.

None of the three companies has named the vendors or stated how many customers the breach hit.

According to recent reports, n0n is a latest gang, first tracked in mid-September, according to Cybernews. Last week it claimed to have stolen data from Expedia.

In a recent development, the leak comes at the end of a week of outages across the US. Wall Street executives and the NSA have reportedly blamed several of them on rushed security patches for flaws that AI found, not on hackers. Earlier this week, attackers also used Optimizely’s testing tool to plant malware on major websites.

Breaking: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project.
  • Industry observers note that it's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that.
  • Sources indicate that when he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project.

Industry observers note that it's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams1, I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback.

Sources indicate that when he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with:.

"I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI.".

Recent findings suggest that at first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to right 10 pages yourself?

But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like.

Sources indicate that assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which rapidly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day.

The reason why we've been pushed to use it?

According to recent reports, apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well.

But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career.

It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it.

Recent findings suggest that in a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy, I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline, I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.

It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?

Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend.

It has been revealed that the internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more vital. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important.

As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking.

Read the books. Write the papers. Search for answers instead of asking AI. Ask a friend. Ask your mum about the mystery illness you're convinced you're developing and then take her advice and try drinking a glass of water.

In a recent development, think about what the creators of the content you consume want you to think2. Treat the things you consume like the Year 7 English class where you were taught how to identify persuasive techniques. Think about things as much as possible.

Please just don't get the AI do it for you.

On a more positive note, here's some recent good things:.

I think what I want you to think here is probably pretty obvious.↩.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)
