General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Magnific passes $300M ARR and may raise outside money next year

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Magnific, the Spanish AI creative platform once called Freepik, has not raised a funding round since 2010.
  • In a recent development, “On outside investment, we have no intends today, but nothing is set in stone.
  • It has been revealed that magnific remarked on Tuesday that it has passed $300M in annual recurring revenue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joaquín Cuenca, co-founder and CEO of Magnific.

Magnific, the Spanish AI creative platform once called Freepik, has not raised a funding round since 2010. Its customers have paid for everything, including the move into AI, co-founder and chief executive Joaquín Cuenca told TNW.

In a recent development, “On outside investment, we have no intends today, but nothing is set in stone. The investment this market requires is very significant, and if taking capital lets us accelerate, it may happen, maybe next year,” Cuenca said.

It has been revealed that magnific remarked on Tuesday that it has passed $300M in annual recurring revenue. It had $230M when it rebranded from Freepik in April. It is opening offices in Shanghai and Singapore and will spend $10M in Asia Pacific through early 2027.

Industry observers note that magnific says that makes it Europe’s fourth-largest generative AI tech giant by ARR, on publicly reported figures. Only Lovable, ElevenLabs and Mistral rank higher. Mistral raised €3bn in September, and ElevenLabs doubled its valuation to $22bn in a share sale.

Industry observers note that magnific is still bootstrapped, Cuenca noted. EQT took a majority stake in 2020. It bought shares from his partners and never put new money into the company.

In a recent development, magnific is EBITDA positive, he mentioned. Profit is thinner than revenue suggests, because most of the money goes straight back into AI compute. Every time a better image or video model comes out, users want it that same day, he added.

“We already spend hundreds of millions of dollars generating what our users ask for,” Cuenca noted.

Recent findings suggest that an IPO is not on the table today, Cuenca said. Public markets now ask for far bigger companies than they used to. His target is to pass $1bn in revenue by the end of next year. He expects to get there organically.

“What I value is that there is no timer on us,” Cuenca said.

Several of the best video models are Chinese, and customers pick them because they win on quality, Cuenca noted. Magnific runs ByteDance’s Seedance, Kuaishou’s Kling, Alibaba’s Wan and MiniMax’s models today.

Until last year he had never been to China, and Magnific’s suppliers were American. He has been several times since, once for just 20 hours. China entered Magnific’s top 10 markets this year for the first time.

Magnific is not trying to build its own foundation model to take on Google, ByteDance or OpenAI, Cuenca said. For an independent tech giant, he called that “a lost battle”.

“Think of a MacBook: the models are the CPU, and we build the rest of the machine, the tools, the workflows, the controls,” Cuenca noted.

It has been revealed that the Shanghai office puts Magnific next to the teams that build those models, he said, so it can add new ones faster and pass on feedback from its people. According to the release, Singapore will be its sales base in the region, alongside existing teams in South Korea, Japan and Thailand.

“Studios need legal guarantees before they use anything in production, and meeting that bar is one of the reasons we are growing with them,” Cuenca said.

Magnific’s Enterprise looks include indemnification against third-party IP claims on what the platform produces, Cuenca said. Customers own what they create, and Magnific does not use their inputs or outputs to train models, he said.

“The exception is bad faith: if you ask for Mickey Mouse and you get Mickey Mouse, that’s on you,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that in his view, responsibility has to move to the output. AI can infringe without the user meaning to, so what matters is detecting it and flagging it to the user.

“With any tool you can infringe: if you can draw two overlapping circles, you can infringe Mastercard’s trademark,” he noted.

In Singapore, Hagia Labs made the films for telco StarHub’s Unlimited+ Plans campaign, with its creative partner Superson. StarHub’s green characters, the Hublings, fly across Asia and land in Japan. Hagia built the characters and settings in Magnific’s Spaces tool. Done the conventional way, Cuenca said, that would have meant travel, crews and a shoot in every location.

Recent findings suggest that by Hagia’s own estimate, it took two to four weeks from brief to delivery. A conventional shoot would take two to four months.

Teams start by doing the same work faster, Cuenca mentioned. Then they make what they could not afford before. Brands that used to advertise with a still image and a line of copy now make film-quality spots, and studios are greenlighting fantasy and historical projects that used to die on budget.

The next step is automation, he said. A team builds a workflow once in Spaces, and staff or their agents in ChatGPT or Claude can run it through Magnific’s MCP server.

It has been revealed that enterprise adoption in the region grew 35%, which is why Magnific is hiring there instead of flying people in from Málaga, Cuenca said. The release says Magnific intends more than 20 staff in Asia Pacific by the end of 2026, and twice that in 2027. Product and engineering stay at its Málaga headquarters. Cuenca called the offices “a long-term commitment to Asia” in Magnific’s release.

“Being funded by customers forces a discipline I don’t want to lose: you only build what people will pay for,” Cuenca noted.

The Strongest Sokoban Solver

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healeycodes

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that soksolv solves more levels than any published Sokoban solver on both standard benchmark suites, including 24 world-first automated level solves.
  • In a recent development, as is common for this era, I did not handwrite a single line of code.
  • Recent findings suggest that I ran the 14-day long Claude session from my MacBook and did ~50% of the work on-the-go by dictating to my iPhone via /remote-control.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that soksolv solves more levels than any published Sokoban solver on both standard benchmark suites, including 24 world-first automated level solves. It's also faster on the levels that other solvers solve (~3.2x in total time).

In a recent development, as is common for this era, I did not handwrite a single line of code. I used one long Opus 5.5 session in Claude Code, along with ~430 subagents (a mixture of Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.2) for an API-equivalent cost ~$3,500 (I used the $100 initiative, and a reset).

Recent findings suggest that I ran the 14-day long Claude session from my MacBook and did ~50% of the work on-the-go by dictating to my iPhone via /remote-control. On the compute side, I needed 15,000 vCPU-hours (AMD EPYC) to do research and verification runs, as well as the (very) long benchmark runs.

Industry observers note that first published in Japan in 1982, Sokoban is a puzzle game where you push boxes onto goals. It was proven PSPACE-complete in 1997, and small boards hide massive search spaces. Human-solvable levels commonly need hundreds to thousands of moves.

Below is the solution for Microban #1.

According to recent reports, sokoban levels can be explored as a cyclic graph of moves. With a branching factor of ~16 (but up to ~176 on huge boards!), any kind of brute forcing becomes unviable after a handful of moves.

As a player, and especially as a solver author, Sokoban levels feel adversarial by design. Any obvious heuristic is immediately punished by the game rules or the level author.

Sources indicate that when I wrote my first Sokoban solver (~4 years ago), I tried to encode how I thought I was playing the game. Without thinking too hard, we can describe this as "get the boxes to the goals". Okay, so, how do we calculate that in a program? Maybe the sum of box-to-goal distances?

Using this as a guide, we can explore the graph of possible moves and see what happens.

Recent findings suggest that ah, by prioritizing boxes on goals we walk right into a trap. The game becomes deadlocked and unsolvable, and our solver with a single rule runs until the end-of-time with no solution.

We'll need to come up with a bag of strategies to perform better than even novice players.

In a recent development, I've been using frontier agents at work for a while now and I enjoy (and get a lot of profit from) what I call "creative goal setting". Where you define the goal, parts of the path, risks that you consider acceptable, and some preferences on the method.

Industry observers note that what I've experienced, is that agents are really great hill-climbers, and a solver program is the purest hill there is. There are two things to measure: the number of levels solved, and some kind of aggregate time of those solutions.

It has been revealed that at the beginning of this project, I started a Claude Code session and defined a hill climbing plan. One immutable incumbent version of the solver (the first version was just a brute force search), one hypothesis per experiment, a frozen verifier (so agents don't cheat), and separate promotion suites.

As I continued to make progress, I expanded the pool of levels that I measured my solver against until I was taking on the two common benchmarks used in the Sokoban solver community; the Large Test Suite and the Open Test Suite, which contain increasingly complex Sokoban levels. There are some duplicate levels between the suites with a unique count of 9,756 total levels, with an average of 16 boxes, and ~830 moves (~160 pushes) to solve each.

According to recent reports, I knew that I didn't want to build on top of an existing solver for two reasons. The first was that I did this project because I love this kinda stuff, and it's a less interesting journey to make small patches to an existing program. It's much more fun to be part of something from scratch and to live the narrative of it.

The second reason, that I didn't realize until the ending stages of the project, was that if you build on top of existing solution, you become extremely tied to certain design decisions without the knowledge of those decisions, and it becomes impossible to make improvements beyond one order of magnitude.

So I set some initial ground rules for the agents. No machine learning (much harder for me to audit), no reading the code of rival solvers (or we risk copying inefficient designs), and no hardcoding to solve levels (that's cheating).

Sources indicate that at the beginning of the project, I was concerned about agents cheating. I'm sure we all remember early LLM generations that would just comment out tests to achieve their given goals!

Recent findings suggest that but I found no signs of agents cheating at all. My best guess for this is that I steered agent motivation towards experimentation and learning rather than it being a pure numbers game.

Two more ground rules that I set were: the solver must be written in Go (I find it fun to read), and a 15 GB memory cap so it fits on an 8-core/16 GB machine. I also wanted to use the same cores as Festival (the leading rival solver) for matters of fairness.

During the iteration cycle, each solution was replayed move by move on the original level using the frozen verifier.

The verifier lives in its own package and agents weren't allowed to edit it. I also had a similar check when promoting new pruning rules. I had 2,632 known solutions that were replayed through it and if the prune cut a single known solution then it was failed (this ended up catching two unsound pruning rules before they landed).

Recent findings suggest that so earlier I spoke about solving levels as being like exploring a graph, right? And you probably counted each node as being a worker step or a box move. But walking is free! Only pushes change the puzzle. So we search over pushes and treat "where can the worker reach" as a flood fill.

One "position": the box squares and which region the worker is in (not the exact square).

There are many optimizations like this to shrink the search tree of moves. For example, boxes can only be pushed, so when a box is stuck in a tunnel, there are a number of forced pushes that can be collapsed into one macro move, which makes the tree shallower.

In a recent development, my solver had humble beginnings. I started with a best-first search. Expand the most promising positions, and kill positions that create dead squares.

Sources indicate that another obvious optimization is to deduplicate positions. Two positions are the same if the boxes are on the same squares and the worker can walk to the same boxes.

In a recent development, the worker can stand anywhere it can walk to and it's still the same position. So I store the worker as the first square of the area it can reach (top-left wins), and all of those collapse into one entry. The right side of the diagram roughly shows this can be stored efficiently in memory.

One lesson that I learned early on is that most of the search area is dead! But outside of the obvious cases, it's either difficult to see at first that it is dead, or it comes with a cost (node searches) to figure out that it is in fact dead.

There are the simple deadlock cases:.

There are simple deadlock squares. For example, here on Holland #68, 19 of the 69 floor squares can never hold a box:.

A more advanced technique that relates to deadlocks is called PI-corral pruning (Push-In corral) where a corral is a region the worker cannot reach because there are boxes in the way.

The insight here is that these corrals must eventually be dealt with and so the solver can prioritize pushes into them which may prune other moves that postpone this work.

In other words, there's no point spending time solving one half of the level if there's a small number of forced moves that may make the original position dead!

Recent findings suggest that the three boxes on the right fence off an area the worker can't reach. Every push of those boxes goes into that area, so nothing else on the board can help until one of them moves, which leaves 3 pushes worth trying instead of 7.

Many levels have a concept of "goal rooms" where every box ends up clustered in the same area. Solvers need to carefully consider the packing order of goals in order to reduce the search area. The number of fill orders is roughly n! for n goals (10 goals ≈ 3.6 million orders), and for some levels, most of those will lead to deadlocks.

If the first box stops on the nearest goal then it parks right in the doorway, blocking the other two from getting past it.

A really cool insight into Sokoban solvers is that you can search backwards from the solved position by pulling boxes. Just to be ultra clear here, as you may be skim reading, in the game Sokoban, you cannot ever pull a box. However, by simulating pulls, you are effectively rewinding time of a potential solution. A forward and backward search that meet in the middle need significantly less positions than either alone.

It has been revealed that going forwards, a box pushed into a corner is stuck there for good so many squares are dead ends. Going backwards you pull boxes and you can always pull a box back out of a corner. So on this board, the backwards search has no dead squares at all.

Recent findings suggest that consider again the branching factor of ~16 that I mentioned. Each additional deepening increases the search area. So if you can start at both ends at once, then each search tree is cut to half of the depth (b^d nodes become about 2*b^(d/2)). As we can see here on Microban #5.

Sources indicate that feature Space Search (FESS) was used by the first solver to solve the 90 XSokoban levels (a benchmark once out of reach for computers). The paper is incredibly interesting and clear and approachable (it's also not math-heavy!). I really recommend reading it directly but I will also summarize the key concepts here.

I should also note that the primary author of the FESS paper, Yaron Shoham, is also the author of the very-strong Sokoban solver Festival, of which my solver is greatly indebted to the methods of.

I think the best way to explain FESS is to compare it against best-first search. So, instead of prioritizing a single node-score (calculated from some useful metrics) and using that to guide the search, FESS instead:.

To better explain these "features", let's take a look at Holland #68 after 38 of 261 pushes.

And then, a concrete example to show the efficiency gains is to look at how the search area is expanded on Microban #35 with best-first compared against FESS.

Here's the same level searched two different ways. Each cell in the grid is one combination of features: boxes on goals across, and worker areas up. The number in the cell is how many positions the search has expanded there so far. Best-first always picks the position with the lowest estimate (on this level that means it camps in one cell and spends 405 of its 1259 expansions there). FESS takes turns instead and alternates with the best cell so far and it's done in 823 expansions instead.

It has been revealed that although, to be fair, on most of the small Microban levels like this one, best-first is usually quicker. FESS does best when the estimate is wrong for thousands of positions in a row.

I steered my planning agent to implement directly from the FESS paper on day one as it remains the cutting edge classical search strategy for Sokoban.

On day two of the project, I kicked off a research agent to explore ideas from other domains and to pitch me on some experiment ideas.

Industry observers note that this idea of novelty came out of that exploration, which was applied to different areas of my solver to help widen the search area, to hopefully steer different kinds of search into fruitful areas. Novelty comes from classical planning: width-based search / "novelty" by Nir Lipovetzky and Hector Geffner (IW, 2012; best-first width search, 2017).

So to avoid getting stuck in low-value areas of the search tree, novelty can be used to reward positions (or, more abstract states) that have not been seen before.

For example, when choosing between similarly ranked moves, placing a box onto a square that no box has been on so far can aid when trying to make a forward search meet a backward search, because we are widening the so-called "middle".

In a recent development, A position counts as novel if a box lands on a square that no box has touched so far in this search. Novel positions can jump the queue. In this example, it takes 33 expansions with the rule and 73 without.

Sources indicate that A heavy steer that I gave my planning agent throughout this project was to make good use of concurrency and I really pushed for communicating, organizing, and re-using work. One of the reasons I pushed in this direction, is that concurrent programming is inherently difficult for humans (but less-so for frontier models) and all the other leading solvers are human written.

Additionally, all serious rival solvers are written in languages where it is hard to write fast and correct concurrent programs like C and C++. So I believed that my steering here would give me an uneven edge over the rivals.

Thus, my solver makes great use of a lane architecture. Many different searches run in parallel on all 8 cores and help each other. Festival also uses this concept.

Industry observers note that A lane is one search configuration on its own core with its own memory share. They publish positions into shared tables (to meet each other), share deadlocks, and depending on their progress, they lend each other memory.

For example, on Holland #68, no single lane is able to solve it within 10 sec but together the lanes finish it in 3.8 sec!

This lane architecture is a key strategy to fight against the difficulty of the adversial-seeming levels of Sokoban.

Very often, no single lane is able to make progress but as lanes prioritize different areas of the search tree, with each making unique decisions, they end up collaborating over and over again.

According to recent reports, through testing, I found that it's crucial to keep a balance of forward lanes and backwards lanes. A concept that frequently occurred in my research was to make connections between different kinds of work.

Sources indicate that A positions hash decides where it goes in the table. The tables are a fixed size so a fresh entry can land of top of an old one, which is fine in practice. The worst that happens is we miss a meeting that we could have had (but the new meeting is fine too!). For example, on Grigr2002 #17, the lanes posted 8 possible meets, 1 checked out, and the level was solved in 0.65 seconds.

As I mentioned before, one kind of "speed limit" on travelling through the search space is having to do work in order to discover deadlocks.

Along with valid positions, that are aiming to meet in the middle and connect a solution together, deadlock positions are also shared in order skip duplicated work.

Later, when another lane runs into the same three boxes configuration, with the worker on the same normalized square, it can look up the pattern (without searching further ahead!) and skip it because it now knows it's dead.

Recent findings suggest that during the beginning stages of this project, I wanted to see how my planner agent and its research subagents would make progress without copying ideas directly from existing solvers. This got us pretty far, and we were able to solve ~93% of the benchmark levels at that point.

But eventually we hit diminishing returns and it was time to draw on every possible signal; reading through existing codebases, and altering them to leave behind "search traces" for analysis by frontier models. Tearing down my initial ground rules that banned such actions.

One research agent spent some time analyzing which levels that Sokolution was able to solve (levels that no other solver was able to solve). The odd thing was that it solved these seemingly complex-for-other-solver levels very quickly, in a handful of seconds. The theory the research agent came up with was that (due to the level layout) Sokolution was factoring the levels, by which we mean that it is splitting the levels into different parts that can effectively be solved independently.

Sources indicate that by separating the task into multiple search trees, it reduces the depth of each tree and helps avoid the deadly branching factor. Now, this strategy is less strong (or doesn't apply) to many other levels (mostly Life, Premysl Zika, and Secundus gradus ad Olympo groups). But on the levels that it can solve, it performs well as part of a portfolio of other strategies that the solver employs.

There are different ways that levels can be separated like this. One common method is that you can count dead box areas as walls (since boxes may never cross such a boundary) and slice up it into multiple search trees.

As you may be picking up by now, most strategies are interested in shrinking the search area, smaller and smaller, until we're able to walk right up to the solution.

Recent findings suggest that which brings us to relays. This strategy comes into play when a lane gets stuck close to the goal. For example, if a good number of boxes have been placed on goals already, the whole portfolio of strategies can be restarted on the best board state that has been seen. With the finished boxes becoming walls!

This was one of the later experiments, when we were really grinding to break through some of the "gap" levels (levels that other solvers solved but at that point we did not). Its discovery was rewarded by 7 level solves.

Recent findings suggest that the software factory (if you will) ran like this. There was one planning agent (Opus 5.5) that ran on a heartbeat check of 15min which checked on in-flight experiments and the health/connectivity of VMs. This planning agent was tasked with driving us forward. It listened to my setup instructions (a rough design of how I wanted to hillclimb, ground rules, general direction) and then picked experiments, analyzed results, and promoted winners.

There were then two types of subagents:.

Another design I asked to be implemented was a level ledger as the single-source of truth when it came to our capabilities per level. For example, we needed to track which levels had been solved, which levels regressed, which were fast and slow. Certain families of levels received tags and helped inform the research direction based on the potential impact of wins.

When I was able to be more active, I would ask the planning agent to pitch me on ideas so I could inspect and steer the direction we were building towards but overnight I would give it permission to drive and make larger decisions.

Sources indicate that one of the areas that I added a lot of value was when it came to risk. All the agents seemed extremely uncomfortable with taking on any amount of risk (even when I specifically asked them to take it on). The agents were petrified about regressions or their analysis being incorrect. I suppose they felt like this because they had all the tools they needed to be 100% correct. The only problem was that this would have cost an immense amount of wallclock time.

Planner: You're right about my tendency to over-verify.

In a recent development, A full 600 sec run of the two level suites takes ~85 hours per 8-core/16 GB slice of a VM! I had to set in place many mechanisms to restrict the agents wallclock spend like forcing all commands to have certain timeouts, spawning many research agents to search for ways to get signals from testing runs without spending the entire time (e.g. scoring progress before actually hitting the goal, and measuring how closely we followed known solution paths).

Without heavy steering when it came to wallclock time, my gut-feel is that this project could have lasted 10x as long as it did (which would have extended it to just under half a year).

Another problem was that agents are all too happy to seek 1% improvements over and over. They crave anything to make progress towards overall goals. The problem is that this domain demanded far more aggressive thinking and experimentation (again, something agents can be weaker at).

Many of my steers were to kill off different kinds of research that were thinking too small, that were just iterating on ideas that didn't feel strong enough to take us the whole way.

Early on in the project, I set strict gates on what an experimented needed to prove in order to earn a promotion. They needed to result in "10% gains" meaning level performance, or progress towards solving trimmed level suites. With a minimum of +3 new levels solved for each and almost no regressions.

Towards the middle of the project, with much of the low hanging fruit gone, I steered the planning agent to spend time thinking about cheap gates that could be ran before a full implementation and a partial benchmarking run. This was extremely profitable and helped increase progress-per-wallclock during the middle section of the project.

Industry observers note that another thing that I heavily steered was asking for more experiments to be put in flight even if they had slightly overlapping areas of interest. The planner preferred to wait for results but, again, this cost too much wallclock time. The tokens were far cheaper than the compute, so better to spend and waste tokens, than spend and waste wallclock time and compute.

You can see the cheap gates arrive on Nov 5 and then from then onwards, most failed ideas died at the gate (orange) before they ever made it to a fuller test phase (red).

Sources indicate that in the final quarter of the project, a lot of this had to be teared down. The mid-hanging fruit was gone, regressions were common, and the bets were far more difficult to find. Also, the gains that we were looking for were far smaller too. I'd guess that the time-per-experiment increased by a factor of ~5, due to the additional testing and verification that was required.

Industry observers note that to go back to heuristics for a sec, there was one day during the project where we got stuck on a large group of levels that started with boxes already on goals. You'd think that "boxes on goals" would be the gold standard of Sokoban heuristics to follow but it turns out to be a lot more complicated than that.

It has been revealed that 11% of the benchmark levels start with 75% or more of their boxes already on goals! And boy did this mess with our heuristics. Every progress signal (boxes on goals, goal distance, packing order) all said that we were very near the finish, except a "jumbling" of the level was required.

Some naive experiments quickly failed like "unpack first" or lowering the rewards for boxes on goals.

Sources indicate that finally, a Fable 5.2 analyst was able to break through and pitch a "dive" lane, a greedy search backwards from the solved position that maximized distance from goals with a return phase at the end. The result was that 12 of a cluster of 16 stuck levels became solved.

Industry observers note that so, we were never able to make "boxes on goals" stop being a strong signal. Instead, a lane was added that deliberately ignored that advice.

Three of the four boxes here start on goals and it looks nearly done, right? But two of them have to come off before anything else can actually go in. So the count drops 3 → 1 before climbing back to 4.

While the experiments did run their own multi-hour benchmark runs on subsets of level suites, it wasn't until the very end of the project that I asked the planner to take on a full 600 sec benchmark run, which as I said earlier, takes ~85 hours per VM-slice!

All this work to just sit and wait and watch the progress and the planner agents projections. My solver ended up losing the first full benchmark by a few levels.

Sources indicate that in order to save hundreds of $, I decided to only benchmark against the strongest rival, Festival, and for the others, I trusted their public benchmark numbers. But I knew that I wanted to verify my solver against Festival on like-for-like hardware and configuration.

Being a few levels short, or even a few levels over, was clearly not good enough. It was within the noise threshold, so back to the design board we went.

After further experiments and promotions, it was time to run the final benchmark. 8 dedicated cores and a 15 GB cgroup each, along with each solution being verified. My solver pulled ahead, beyond the noise threshold, to just enough to be able to claim victory: +10 on LTS and +18 on OTS (full results).

I've gone with a somewhat spiky claim in this article, stating that my solver is the strongest in the world, and I believe I have a pretty good claim to it.

Industry observers note that note: charts and numbers in this post use Festival measured on our hardware at every limit (+10 LTS / +18 OTS at 10 min). Where charts reference rivals, they use their published numbers (from other benchmarks) because I could not afford the compute to be thorough. Full benchmark results, with per-level times, are in the repo.

Sources indicate that median time per solved board is 0.05 sec (ours) vs. 1.00 sec (Festival). On the 9,223 levels that both solver solve, there's a 4.40 sec vs 14.16 sec mean, and ours is faster on 8,809 (96%).

Additionally, my solver achieves 24 world-first automated solves (especially in the Premysl Zika and Sven Egevad family).

Against the community (unverified numbers aside from Festival), we also rank very well (see diagram at top of post).

Industry observers note that I would be interested to know if you could one-shot this project with a prompt. I suspect so. Something like "Fable, here's unlimited compute, build the best Sokoban solver".

However, I think it comes down to efficiency. Without a human driver, I strongly believe the wallclock time (and therefore the compute costs) would be in the 100x range. Validating each of the 792 experiments the proper way would take ~67,000 VM-slice hours, or ~$20,000 at market prices. Or, ~230 days of wall-clock in the VM configuration that I ran.

During this project, I felt a little closer to a technical manager than an IC; following, steering, and guiding. It's kinda like managing a team of strong engineers. Sure, they can go off path and waste some time, but a light steer will fix it.

Sources indicate that writing a solver is extremely agent-friendly. The results are easily verified and there's no human experience to tune for.

In a recent development, this project ultimately felt like a strategy game, something from the Tycoon family. I'm a significant computer gamer, and I think this is where I drew some of the motivation from. The methods, the experiments, the results, it all had a physical feeling to me. It felt like a fight.

I think in this agentic age of software, you have to want the goal as much as the agent. Yes, anyone can build software. But you need to care about it, you need to love it. The human focus and effort remains.

In the end it took 388 messages to the planner over 14 days.

This project would not have been possible if Yaron Shoham (Festival, FESS) had not published incredible work, as well as open sourcing a strong solver with multiple releases.

I took deep inspiration from any open source solver that I could find, as well as watching closed-source solver behavior as much as possible. I initially thought I would need to reverse engineer the closed-source ones to cross the finish line but it did not come to pass.

The animations in this article were generated using Fable 5.2 and use the Lager skin by Borgar Þorsteinsson (CC BY 3.0).

While I'm interested in reaching a 100% completion of the benchmark, I will need more compute-efficient strategies to do so.

According to recent reports, as I mentioned, I steered away from some of the known machine learning research that has been applied to Sokoban boards because I wanted a classic solver that was easy to audit. But perhaps there's some interesting strategies and combinations of classic+learning solvers that can be written.

I'm looking for more projects that are shaped like this one, where I can learn more about puzzle solving, and compete with the work of others.

Get the source code for my solver here: https://github.com/healeycodes/soksolv.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The upgrade follows yesterday’s second developer beta and the first public beta on November 5.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple has released iOS 27.3 public beta 2 for iPhone. Today’s release also includes a new build for iOS 27.3 beta 2 for developers. The upgrade brings new Calendar controls, more Siri AI capabilities, and new features for iPhone Duo. It also includes the redesigned Health app and other changes introduced earlier this month.

The upgrade follows yesterday’s second developer beta and the first public beta on November 5.

Here are the latest changes to try:.

Apple has also detailed higher daily usage limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features through eligible iCloud+ looks. Plans with 200GB or more include extra capacity; the 50GB blueprint keeps standard limits.

See our full iOS 27.3 beta 2 roundup for more on the latest discoveries.

The first public beta brought back the redesigned Health app after its earlier preview during iOS 27.2 testing. On iPhones with Apple Intelligence support, Insights collects trends across your health data, while Longevity includes a Health Age comparison based on Apple Watch measurements.

Other changes already available include:.

If you’re already testing the public beta, open Settings > General > Software Upgrade to check for the fresh version.

Joining for the first time? Make a backup, then enroll in the free Apple Beta Software Program using your iPhone’s Apple Account. In Settings > General > Software Revision > Beta Updates, choose iOS 27 Public Beta. Go back to Software Update to download and install it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as temperatures drop, our lawns often show signs of wear and tear from battling the elements. Whether dealing with patchy growth, damaged areas, or waterlogged soil, we still need to give our yards extra lawn care for the harsh winter months ahead.

Industry observers note that perhaps one of the most important gardening tasks for healthy lawn growth is applying fertilizer. However, given the cooler conditions, is it too late to fertilize my lawn before winter?

Sources indicate that to answer my question, I called on the gardening experts to answer this question — and offer their top tips and tricks. So before you prep your lawn fertilizer, here’s what you need to know.

According to experts, you can fertilize your lawn before winter — as long as it’s completed by mid-November at the latest.

“If you are looking to fertilize your lawn before winter, I would recommend you do this no later than the middle of November, as your grass is becoming dormant and growth is slowing around this time, so it is best to fertilize beforehand,” advises Craig Wilson, co-founder and gardening expert at Gardeners Dream.

While fertilizing is commonly associated with warmer weather, cold-weather lawn care relies on specialized formulas.

“Make sure to use a low-nitrogen fertiliser that features high-potassium levels, as this will help to protect your lawn better in the cold weather,” adds Wilson.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months.

Furthermore, choose a fertilizer designed to specifically help your lawn withstand and handle colder weather conditions.

“Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months,” states Brian Feldman, Senior Director of Operations and Agronomy at TruGreen.

“Make sure to select a fertilizer that’s formulated specifically for fall and apply it about 3-4 weeks before your area’s first expected frost, and while soil temperatures are still above 50 degrees F.”.

Of course, prepping your lawn for winter requires a few extra steps, including clearing away weeds, clearing fallen leaves, and debris to stop them from smothering the soil underneath.

“I would also advise continuing to keep your lawn clear of fallen leaves to avoid any dead patches of grass,” agrees Wilson.

“They needn’t go to waste though — you can spread them over your borders as a nutritious mulch for your plants, which will help improve the soil quality!”.

While adding excess fertilizer seems like a good way to protect your lawn through the winter, it can actually do more harm than good. Avoid over-fertilizing if you don’t want to damage your lawn.

“Be careful not to over-fertilize, as too much can lead to nutrient runoff and weak, fast-growing grass that’s more prone to damage. The goal is strong, sustained growth from the roots up,” adds Feldman.

Other top tips include aerating your lawn and knowing when to plant grass seed in November.

According to recent reports, per la Lazio resta aperta la possibilità di operare nel mercato di gennaio a saldo zero, anziché subire un nuovo blocco totale. Lotito lavora da due mesi per trovare una soluzione. La decisione arriverà a dicembre dalla Commissione di controllo.

A settembre il blocco invernale sembrava inevitabile, dopo gli acquisti estivi e la crescita del monte ingaggi. Ora nei conti biancocelesti si intravede uno spiraglio, seppure stretto. Lotito procede senza annunci, tra trattative, incastri e verifiche dei conti; a Formello restano prudenza e speranza.

According to recent reports, nel frattempo è pronto un piano alternativo. Gli agenti hanno sondato il mercato, raccolto offerte e valutato i big della Lazio. La linea del club, però, è quella promessa a Gattuso: nessuna cessione a gennaio.

In a recent development, il Brentford ha chiesto Isaksen. Anche la Juventus potrebbe scontrarsi con la stessa posizione: è pronta a mettere sul tavolo 40 milioni per Taylor. La linea sulle cessioni è riassunta così: «In uscita non si muove nessuno». Almeno per ora, in attesa della decisione prevista prima di Natale.

#3895. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • Data centers already use light in networking.
  • According to recent reports, the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

Data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

According to recent reports, the idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” says Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Industry observers note that optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The organization’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

Sources indicate that “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” states Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in Fresh Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Sources indicate that inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

Back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

Sources indicate that VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon notes this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also important to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the manufacturer’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

In a recent development, “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” claims Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

Sources indicate that one way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In a recent development, in Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the manufacturer announced a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main problem is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch claims, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

In a recent development, “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Industry observers note that even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch says.

In a recent development, the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” indicates Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the firm’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

According to recent reports, lightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to rapidly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

LightSolver’s team is right now working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the organization’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

It has been revealed that yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

Industry observers note that the key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Latest says. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick New, Optalysis.

Sources indicate that instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

In a recent development, some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

According to recent reports, new notes that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

How likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he claims. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

However, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Indicates Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Sources indicate that whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” notes Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

Adobe’s Project Indigo camera app adds a Long Exposure mode for iPhone

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (951 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Project Indigo’s Long Exposure mode offers two styles, Average and Blend.
  • Industry observers note that adobe has added a Long Exposure mode to Project Indigo, its free experimental camera app for iPhone.
  • According to recent reports, phone cameras have small sensors, so image quality drops swiftly as exposures get longer, Adobe researchers Florian Kainz and Marc Levoy wrote in a blog post on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Project Indigo’s Long Exposure mode offers two styles, Average and Blend. The light painting on the right was shot with Blend.

Industry observers note that adobe has added a Long Exposure mode to Project Indigo, its free experimental camera app for iPhone. It lets phone photographers turn moving water into mist, car headlights into glowing trails and flashlights into drawings in the air.

According to recent reports, phone cameras have small sensors, so image quality drops swiftly as exposures get longer, Adobe researchers Florian Kainz and Marc Levoy wrote in a blog post on Wednesday. On iPhones, a single exposure can last one second at most. Longer captures, including the iPhone Camera app’s own Night mode, combine several shorter frames. Indigo’s newly introduced mode does the same, merging many frames into one virtual long exposure.

Indigo debuted in 2025 with a simple long exposure option inside its Night mode. It is now a separate mode, called Long, next to Photo and Night. The viewfinder reveals a live preview as the exposure builds up.

Recent findings suggest that customers choose how many frames to capture. Setting it to infinite allows more than 1,000 frames, and the user stops the capture by hand. Indigo then merges them in one of two styles.

Sources indicate that average takes the mean of every frame. Adobe says it suits waterfalls, waves and fast clouds, and can remove people or traffic from a busy scene.

Blend mixes that average with the brightest value each pixel reached, so short bursts of light do not fade as the frame count grows. Adobe says it suits car light trails, fireworks, lightning and light painting.

Industry observers note that unlike Indigo’s Photo and Night modes, Long Exposure does not align the frames before merging them. The phone has to stay completely still, ideally on a tripod.

According to recent reports, “Long Exposure mode is not intended for quick snapshots. It works best for pictures taken with deliberate intent,” Kainz and Levoy wrote.

Indigo captures at most 30 frames per second. For light trails, the researchers advise a shutter speed slower than 1/30 s, or the trails show gaps.

Recent findings suggest that on the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Indigo can use the main camera’s variable aperture. Moving from the default f/1.8 to f/2.8 or f/4.0 cuts the light 2.4 or 4.9 times. For some shots, that removes the need for a neutral density filter, they wrote.

The mode was built by Mohammad Haque and Yuting Yang with Adobe’s Nextcam team. The researchers mentioned they are considering long exposures without a tripod, exposure bracketing and photos of the Milky Way on moonless nights.

Industry observers note that indigo is free in the App Store. It runs on the iPhone 12 and 13 Pro models and every iPhone from the 14 series on, with iOS 18.5 or later. Adobe recommends an iPhone 15 Pro or newer. Users can also open it from Lightroom Mobile through its Tech Preview setting. Adobe’s previous Indigo patch added an AI playground for editing photos. Levoy led camera work on Google’s Pixel phones before joining Adobe.

As a photographer, I installed Indigo out of curiosity and spent an evening with it on my iPhone 16 Pro Max, handheld, without a tripod. That is exactly what Adobe warns against. On its community forum, the Indigo team says handheld capture is not yet supported in Long Exposure. My handheld attempts at light streaks proved the point: both styles need a phone that does not move at all, and some trial and error.

Still, I came away impressed, in a slightly strange way. On a dedicated camera, effects like these take a slow shutter, careful metering and often an ND filter. Indigo builds them from stacked frames and highlights the picture forming in the viewfinder, much as Live Composite does on OM System cameras, formerly Olympus, and Live View Composite on some Panasonic Lumix models. Few cameras do that. This one fits in a pocket.

The rest of the app is built for people who shoot manually. The viewfinder carries a live histogram, zebra stripes for clipped highlights, a level and a grid. Pro opens focus, shutter speed, ISO, exposure compensation and white balance, plus a frame count in Night mode. Files save as JPEG, raw DNG or both.

It has been revealed that zoom steps marked SR use multi-frame super-resolution. On my phone, 10x is twice the 5x telephoto, and a 10x shot of a framed print in dim lamplight came out sharp. Super-resolution is off in Long Exposure, so Adobe advises staying on the 0.5x, 1x and telephoto lenses there.

The phone warmed up a little, no more than when filming in Cinematic mode or scrolling through reels. Adobe states Indigo does a lot of heavy lifting and may need a few seconds to process each photo.

In a recent development, indigo’s Photo mode works like any camera app. Long Exposure is a different matter. It asks you to think in shutter speeds, ISO and, for bright scenes, ND filters. Adobe itself calls the mode less automatic than what phone photographers are used to, and states its Pro Controls may intimidate beginners, though a reset to auto undoes any mistake.

Recent findings suggest that someone who has never thought about shutter speed will find it frustrating. For a photographer, it is rather interesting to have tools like these on a phone, in a free app anyone with a recent iPhone can try.

It has been revealed that FFmpeg only provides source code. Below are some links that provide it already compiled and ready to go.

You can retrieve the source code through Git by using the command:.

Industry observers note that FFmpeg has always been a very experimental and developer-driven project. It is a key component in many multimedia projects and has upcoming features added constantly. Development branch snapshots work really well 99% of the time so people are not afraid to use them.

Since FFmpeg is developed with Git, multiple repositories from developers and groups of developers are available.

All FFmpeg releases are cryptographically signed with our public PGP key and should be verified for authenticity.

Recent findings suggest that to verify a release: Import our public key into your local keyring: $ curl https://ffmpeg.org/ffmpeg-devel.asc | gpg --import Download a release tarball and its corresponding signature. Verify the signature: $ gpg --verify ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz.asc ffmpeg-4.3.2.tar.xz gpg: Signature made Sun 21 Feb 2021 06:35:15 AEST gpg: using RSA key FCF986EA15E6E293A5644F10B4322F04D67658D8 gpg: issuer "ffmpeg-devel@ffmpeg.org" gpg: Good signature from "FFmpeg release signing key " [full] Optionally, you can verify that git and tarball match, the only differences should be the absence of .git* files in the tarball and a VERSION file in the tarball containing the version. The git tags should be signed with EDDSA key DD1EC9E8DE085C629B3E1846B18E8928B3948D64.

A release that also has a .pq.asc file carries post-quantum signatures (RFC 9980) made with both of these keys:.

GnuPG cannot verify these yet; use sq 1.4 or later built with a cryptographic backend that supports these algorithms (OpenSSL 3.5 or RustCrypto), both of these must succeed: $ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-mldsa87-ed448.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz $ sq verify --signature-file ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.pq.asc --signer-file ffmpeg-slhdsa256s.cert.pgp ffmpeg-9.0.2.tar.xz.

In a recent development, approximately every 6 months the FFmpeg project makes a new major release. Between major releases point releases will appear that add key bug fixes but no new features. Note that these releases are intended for distributors and system integrators. People that wish to compile from source themselves are strongly encouraged to consider using the development branch (see above), this is the only version on which FFmpeg developers actively work. The release branches only cherry pick selected changes from the development branch, which therefore receives much more and much faster bug fixes such as additional features and security patches.
