Latest Update: Claude vs. ChatGPT: 5 key differences that could change which AI you use

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that chatGPT and Claude are two of the biggest names in AI, and both have become significantly more capable within the last few months.
  • ChatGPT has evolved into an all-purpose assistant with tools for everything from image generation and voice conversations to coding and research.
  • I've spent plenty of time testing both, and while there's considerable overlap between what they can do, there are some differences worth understanding before deciding which one deserves your time and money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that chatGPT and Claude are two of the biggest names in AI, and both have become significantly more capable within the last few months. Whether you need help writing an email, researching a topic, creating an app or managing your workload, both chatbots can handle far more than simple questions and answers. But despite their similarities, OpenAI and Anthropic have taken different approaches to building their AI assistants.

ChatGPT has evolved into an all-purpose assistant with tools for everything from image generation and voice conversations to coding and research. Claude has become hyper-focused on writing, programming and helping people complete more complicated tasks through its growing collection of productivity tools.Now that Anthropic has gone public, people are beginning to wonder what is so special about the firm's AI known as Claude.

I've spent plenty of time testing both, and while there's considerable overlap between what they can do, there are some differences worth understanding before deciding which one deserves your time and money.

Here are five of the biggest differences between Claude and ChatGPT.

Claude has developed a reputation for producing natural-sounding text that is especially true for longer pieces. It's also good at following detailed writing instructions and maintaining a consistent tone and style across multiple rounds of editing.

And while ChatGPT is no slouch when it comes to writing, either, it has the advantage of flexibility. You can ask it to rewrite something in five different tones, brainstorm headline ideas or transform a complicated explanation into something a beginner can understand.So, while Claude may be the better starting point for someone writing a novel or polishing a lengthy document, ChatGPT is especially useful when experimenting with different approaches.

Industry observers note that of course, writing quality is subjective. The results also depend on which model you're using and how clearly you explain what you want.

One of ChatGPT's biggest advantages is how many different types of tasks it can handle within the same experience.

Alongside traditional text conversations, ChatGPT supports image generation and editing. You can describe a picture you want to create, upload an existing image to change its appearance or use the chatbot to develop visual concepts.

ChatGPT also offers voice conversations, so customers can speak naturally with the assistant instead of typing everything into a chat window.

Claude has expanded its creative capabilities, too, particularly through Artifacts, which lets owners create interactive content, visualizations and applications.

However, Claude's creative tools are more focused on building useful digital experiences than generating standalone images.

For anyone who regularly switches between writing, visual creation and spoken conversations, ChatGPT offers a more versatile experience.

Coding or "vibe coding" has become one of the biggest battlegrounds between Anthropic and OpenAI.

Claude Code is Anthropic's coding agent, designed to work directly with codebases, understand existing projects, make changes and help developers solve complicated programming problems.

It has become particularly popular with developers who want an AI assistant that can work inside their existing development environment.

OpenAI's answer is Codex, which can also navigate repositories, write code, fix bugs and handle development tasks.

Both tools go well beyond generating snippets of code in a chatbot. They can take on larger assignments and work through multiple steps of a project.

The biggest difference is often how developers prefer to work. Claude Code has strong roots in terminal-based development, while Codex offers workflows across different development environments and agent-based tasks.

Industry observers note that for casual people who occasionally need help building a website or debugging a script, either chatbot can be useful. Developers working on larger projects may find that their preferred coding agent becomes the deciding factor. Personally, I tend to hit my usage limits and blast through tokens faster with Claude Code,.

One of the most interesting changes to Claude is Anthropic's growing focus on turning the chatbot into a coworker.

According to recent reports, with Cowork, Claude can take on more complicated assignments involving files, documents and connected tools. Rather than walking through every step in a conversation, people can describe the outcome they want and let Claude work through the assignment.

For example, someone could ask Claude to organize project materials, work through a collection of documents or prepare files for a presentation.

ChatGPT is moving in a similar direction with its own agent capabilities, including ChatGPT Work and Codex.

The difference is how these experiences are organized and presented to users. Anthropic has emphasized the idea of Claude as a digital coworker that can take responsibility for larger assignments. OpenAI has built a broader ecosystem that includes conversational assistance, research, creative tools and specialized agents.

Neither approach is inherently better, but if you're looking for an AI assistant to do more than answer questions, knowing the difference is crucial.

Price is another consideration, particularly if you're not sure how often you'll use an AI chatbot.

Both companies offer free access, although usage limits and available features vary.

It has been revealed that chatGPT Plus and Claude Pro each cost $20 per month in the United States. ChatGPT also offers a lower-priced Go subscription for $8 per month, giving users another option between the free and Plus tiers.

Claude offers annual billing for Pro, which can reduce the effective monthly cost for consumers willing to commit to a full year.

Sources indicate that of course, usage limits, access to more powerful models and included tools can make one subscription more valuable than another. For example, if you think you're going to be creating more images and want that type of creativity from a model, than you'll want to go with ChatGPT. At the same time, if you're a casual user looking for an affordable upgrade, ChatGPT offers more flexibility in its pricing. But, if you rely heavily on Claude's writing and coding capabilities, Pro may be worth the investment.

Recent findings suggest that here's some good news: you don't have to choose between one or the other. Because ChatGPT offers so much for free, it might be worth sticking with it. But, if you find yourself going through tokens much faster with Claude, you might want to consider bumping up your subscription to a paid tier. I use both agents for different things, which brings me to another point. The bigger question is what you want your AI assistant to do.

Claude is particularly appealing for people who spend their days writing, coding or working through complicated projects. Its emphasis on natural language and increasingly capable agent tools makes it a strong choice for serious productivity work.

ChatGPT offers a broader experience. Between image generation, voice conversations, research, coding and its growing collection of productivity features, it's designed to serve as an assistant for almost anything.

Industry observers note that if you want one AI chatbot that can handle the widest variety of everyday tasks, start with ChatGPT. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I've been a fan of “Percy Jackson” for as long as I can remember. I still remember picking up the books for the first time as a kid and getting completely swept up in Rick Riordan’s world of Greek mythology, monsters and teenage demigods. It’s a franchise I’ve had a soft spot for ever since, so seeing it find a latest audience through Disney’s adaptation has been a real treat. And now, somehow, we’re already heading into "Percy Jackson and the Olympians" season 3. I can’t quite believe how swiftly that’s come around, but I’m certainly not complaining.

Recent findings suggest that season 3 adapts “The Titan's Curse,” the third book in Riordan’s beloved series. This time, Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri) find themselves on a dangerous mission to rescue Annabeth (Leah Sava Jeffries), who has gone missing following an encounter with a mysterious newly introduced threat. With the fate of Olympus hanging in the balance, Percy must contend with powerful enemies and a prophecy that could change everything. It’s another significant adventure for the young demigods, but one that comes with considerably higher stakes.

Industry observers note that I’ve watched the first four episodes of season 3, and there’s plenty to get excited about. While the show still has the humor, friendship and sense of adventure that made me fall in love with the books in the first place, this latest chapter feels noticeably more mature. It’s an encouraging step forward for the Disney+ series, and one that makes me even more invested in seeing where these characters go next. Here’s what I thought of the first four episodes.

In a recent development, I’m Alix, a lifelong horror nerd who loves watching, reviewing and writing about the latest movies and TV shows. When I’m not working through my ever-growing horror watchlist, I’m covering the biggest releases across streaming and film, including "VisionQuest" on Disney+, "The Institute" season 2 on MGM+, and "Guarding Stars" on Netflix.

According to recent reports, season 3 of “Percy Jackson and the Olympians” wastes little time setting a darker, more action-packed tone. It opens with Thalia Grace (Tamara Smart) hunting for Luke (Charlie Bushnell) in a parking garage, where she finds herself battling a dangerous monster. Percy soon crashes into the fight. Thalia isn’t particularly thrilled about needing his help, which establishes some immediate friction between the two demigods. The opening also introduces the season’s central mission, with Annabeth explaining that she needs Thalia’s help to rescue two young demigods, siblings Nico (Levi Chrisopulos) and Bianca di Angelo (Olive Abercrombie).

Book readers will understand the significance of these characters straight away, while show-only viewers will get a better idea as the season unfolds. Thankfully, the first episode doesn't take long to get the main story moving, either, as Annabeth is abducted, triggering Percy’s fatal flaw: his unwavering loyalty. He’s determined to get her back, no matter how dangerous the quest becomes. That sense of danger carries through the first four episodes, and I think it’s one of the season’s biggest improvements.

Sources indicate that with the group getting older and the looming threat of war becoming increasingly difficult to ignore, the show feels noticeably more mature in its storytelling. Percy and his friends are exposed to greater dangers, and there’s a stronger sense that their actions could have serious consequences. It’s also great to see the series developing Percy’s abilities, particularly his control over water. His powers have felt somewhat underexplored in previous seasons, so watching him become more confident and capable with them is a welcome change. He’s clearly getting stronger, and I hope the remaining episodes continue to build on that.

Of course, you can't talk about “Percy Jackson” without mentioning Percabeth, and I know plenty of fans are just as invested in Percy and Annabeth’s developing relationship as they are in the Greek mythology. Thankfully, season 3 gives us a little more to enjoy on that front. It’s still very much a slow burn, with neither quite ready to acknowledge that their feelings might be more than friendship, but there’s a growing awareness that something special is there. The dance scene in episode 1 is a particularly lovely example of this. I suspect season 3 will give Percabeth fans plenty to get excited about.

In a recent development, based on the first four episodes, season 3 is probably the strongest “Percy Jackson” season yet. I particularly appreciate is how much more attention is given to the emotional baggage these teenagers carry as the children of some incredibly powerful figures, many of whom seem largely uninterested in their own kids’ lives. including Thalia’s complicated relationship with Zeus. We get more of an insight into how these circumstances fuel their trauma and motives.

It gives the series a little more emotional depth without losing sight of the fun. The visual effects are also stronger, with the action sequences feeling grander and more cinematic than before. There’s a real sense that the show is becoming more ambitious with each season, and these early episodes have me excited to see what’s next. If the remaining episodes maintain this momentum, “Percy Jackson” could reach a whole newly introduced level, and I can only hope Disney+ has more seasons covering the rest of the books in store.

The first two episodes of "Percy Jackson" season 3 is streaming on Disney+, with the final six episodes releasing in pairs every Friday through December 11, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of users. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the organization’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the organization has also introduced latest restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple announced plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give consumers more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Industry observers note that over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted fresh job listings that offer a closer look at its intends to develop autonomous AI agents:.

In a recent development, in one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

Sources indicate that “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Recent findings suggest that today’s report on the latest job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the firm could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its looks for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how swiftly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally rolled out its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

Marked down from $64 to just $22, this retro-1990s Casio digital watch features an onboard step counter and Bluetooth antenna for automatic time adjustments.

According to recent reports, hidden behind the screen of this seemingly ordinary digital watch is a Bluetooth antenna. Why would a dumb watch need Bluetooth? To pair it with your smartphone, of course. Once paired, the Casio WSB1000 automatically corrects the time based on your smartphone’s clock.

It has been revealed that this means there’s no need to fuss with resetting the time when traveling across time zones. The bare-bones smartphone app can also be used to set or cancel an alarm on the watch, a timer, a stopwatch, and other basic functions.

Bluetooth, meanwhile, is used to ping that step-count data back to your smartphone.

With onboard Bluetooth and automatic step-count tracking, battery life must be pretty short? Surprisingly, no. Casio indicates that the common drugstore CR2016 battery in the watch should keep it powered for approximately two years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although the iPhone Duo was released just this fall, Apple is finalizing the foldable’s second generation. According to a Bloomberg report, Apple has already created prototypes for the second iPhone Duo, codenamed V78, and some include a sought-after feature: Face ID.

Apple reportedly wants to bring Face ID to the foldable, potentially integrating it into the outer display. However, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman notes that Apple appears to be running out of time to finalize its intends for the Duo ahead of a fall 2027 launch.

Also: iPhone Duo review: Hard to recommend, even harder to put down.

In a recent development, iPhone launch events typically take place in early September, when Apple releases its newly introduced smartphone lineups. To have the iPhones ready for sale on the heels of their announcement, Apple must manufacture the new models well before the launch event.

Because of this timeline concern, Face ID isn’t guaranteed for the iPhone Duo 2, though it could come to a third generation instead.

Other planned uogrades — including an Action Button, a telephoto camera, and a thinner, lighter construction — are also noted in the report.

Apple reportedly wants to add an Action Button, the customizable button that performs an action when pressed. The iPhone Duo 2 may combine the Action Button and the Camera Control buttons into a single button, providing a useful physical shortcut instead of adding a new button.

The report indicates that many people don’t use the camera control button as often as Apple expected. Combining the camera and action buttons gives Apple the real estate necessary to add both options in an already constrained space.

Apple also wants to incorporate a telephoto camera into the iPhone Duo, though this is likely to happen in one of the next couple of generations. A telephoto camera would give users greater flexibility to zoom in and capture clear photos of distant objects, which would be an upgrade to the Duo’s photography features.

It has been revealed that technically, equipping the Duo with a telephoto camera is feasible, but the biggest obstacle is space constraints. A telephoto camera needs more room than a wide-angle one, since it requires additional optical elements to magnify distant objects.

Apple already uses a tetraprism design in its Pro iPhones, which allows a longer optical path without too much physical depth.

Apple also wants to reduce the weight and thickness of the iPhone Duo, which is legitimately clunky and cumbersome. To do this, Apple needs to balance the large internal and outer displays, battery capacity, camera array, and the hinge mechanism.

Also: The iPhone Action Button you’re hardly using has a superpower.

For many users, reducing the weight and thickness of a passport-sized foldable could matter more in buying decisions than adding another button or camera.

Gurman’s latest report doesn’t mention any planned changes for the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism, even after concerns with the first generation’s durability. With manufacturing deadlines fast approaching, however, it’s unlikely that Apple will be able to make changes to the Duo 2 based on consumer feedback. More than likely, these changes would come with the third-generation model.

It has been revealed that CNET tested the iPhone Duo’s hinge mechanism and found that, after around 440,000 cycles, the hinge stopped opening flat on its own. Loosening and other signs of wear were evident after 390,000 folds.

Also: The best iPhone Duo cases: Expert recommended.

Given the thinner, lighter construction of a future Duo model, one could assume that changes to the hinge and the foldable’s internal structure are imminent, but this has not been confirmed.

Sources indicate that because Apple will not have enough time to gather feedback on the iPhone Duo before the manufacturing deadlines for the iPhone Duo 2, I don’t expect the second-generation iPhone Duo to be significantly different from its predecessor. We do expect a thinner iPhone Duo 2 and a way to incorporate the Action and Camera buttons.

With user permission, ChatGPT Health connects to Apple Health and supported medical records to provide useful context to health-related questions. The feature presently works in the United States on iPhone, iPad, and the web.

However, a recent notice from OpenAI points to ChatGPT Health coming to many more platforms.

For instance, ChatGPT Health will soon work with the desktop version of ChatGPT for the first time. This would bring ChatGPT Health to the Mac app.

OpenAI also says ChatGPT Health will work with Android, ChatGPT Sites, and ChatGPT Dots, the firm’s proactive assistant feature.

The move follows a similar pattern with the rollout of ChatGPT Finances, which was originally limited to mobile and the web before recently reaching the Mac app as well.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

It has been revealed that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash fresh competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

It has been revealed that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

It has been revealed that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

It has been revealed that RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

In a recent development, recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The organization’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

Sources indicate that but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

According to recent reports, an intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

It has been revealed that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s currently receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

Recent findings suggest that there’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

In a recent development, but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

In a recent development, at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s crucial to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

In a recent development, last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

In a recent development, though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the firm’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

It has been revealed that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted looks for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

Jujutsu Primer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3361 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ethanlowman

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.
  • Industry observers note that jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows.
  • In a recent development, if you work in a Git repository, you can try it today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu (jj) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.

Industry observers note that jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover newly introduced powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.

In a recent development, if you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository, so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git.

According to recent reports, personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.

Official installation instructions are here, but here are a few common methods:.

In an existing git repository, run:.

From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.

To set your user details globally, run commands like these:.

You can edit jj’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:.

In a recent development, in addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:.

A commit, also called a revision, is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.

It has been revealed that when using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.

Industry observers note that the IDs on the left hand side (royxmykx and kpqxywon) are change IDs, which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.

Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example, instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon, we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k.

We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show, using its short prefix 2.

It has been revealed that many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta. See configuration docs if you’re interested.

Let’s take another look at our commit graph:.

On commit 849165bc, you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy, or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:.

jj show demonstrates commit details and a diff, which is empty here. $ jj show Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk Author : Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) Committer: Ethan Lowman (2026-11-15 12:17:12) (no description set).

jj status demonstrates repo state with diff stats. $ jj status The working copy has no changes. Working copy (@) : kpqxywon 849165bc (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-): royxmykx 2bea5e3d main | Adjust config.

It has been revealed that jj diff works much like git diff. Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.

This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show, we see this:.

You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty). The new commit ID for @ is 66b59f20, since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon. jj has no staging area like in git, so we don’t have to manually add files. When we run a jj command to inspect or modify repo state after editing files, jj automatically snapshots the working copy as a new physical commit for the relevant logical change.

Let’s give this change a description (also called a commit message). We can either run jj desc, which opens an editor, or provide it directly with -m.

Notice again that the commit ID has changed, since the hash covers the commit message, but the change ID has remained stable.

Now, let’s say we’re ready to use this latest feature, and we want to organize that change in a separate commit. We can create a new commit with jj new:.

In a recent development, we’ve created an empty change nlrtlrxv on top of kpqxywon. jj status reflects that we are editing this latest revision which does not yet differ from its parent.

In a recent development, jj commit is a shorthand for this common jj desc and jj newly introduced combo. Let’s make another change to use our new feature, and commit it.

Sources indicate that to inspect the commit we just created (n), we can no longer use the bare jj show, which defaults to showing @. We have to pass the revision we want to inspect:.

We can describe empty commits to record intent before starting work. Let’s create a upcoming commit on top of k to remind ourselves that we need to document the feature.

A separate jj desc would also work just fine instead of the -m flag on jj new. Here’s the current commit graph:.

Note how we’ve created branching commits without creating a named branch. This highlights a major difference between jj’s branchless model and git’s branch-centric model of organizing work streams. Instead of juggling your work-in-progress on branches, you work on a graph of commits. Once ready to share, you push branches to a Git forge from your commit graph (more on that later).

A revset, an idea borrowed from Mercurial, is an expression that selects a set of revisions from the commit graph. Most jj commands accept revsets in their arguments. When we ran jj new k, the argument k was actually a trivial revset that resolved to the single change with ID kpqxywon. The jj log command has an -r flag that we can use to preview a revset. Some demonstrative examples follow.

Commits between r and @, inclusive:.

Commits authored by ethan@example.com that also have ID k or q:.

I’ll defer to the official documentation for exhaustive detail. The Revsets language specification is easily my most referenced jj documentation page, so I would recommend skimming it to see what’s possible.

Let’s say in the course of documenting our feature in qwyusntz we realized we made a mistake in the implementation in parent change kpqxywon. We don’t need to manually commit or stash changes to switch tasks. We simply switch our working copy to kpqxywon with jj edit:.

Our working copy once again reveals the changes from kpqxywon.

jj hasn’t lost track of the changes above our working copy, including our most recent edits to q:.

Instead of switching commits with jj edit k, we could have run jj edit @-. The revset @- is evaluated before switching the working copy, so this moves to the parent commit. The built-in commands jj next [--edit] and jj prev [--edit] provide another way to move up and down a stack of commits.

If we edit files in the working copy, the descendant commits will be automatically rebased upon the next jj invocation. For example, if we edit my_new_feature’s implementation in main.py and then run jj log, we’ll see that changes k, n, and q all get fresh commit IDs. jj also tells us that it performed a rebase.

If the automatic rebase happened to cause merge conflicts, jj doesn’t require us to fix them immediately, like git rebase would. Instead, jj records that the commit is conflicted and lets you carry on with your current task. This is massively helpful to reduce mental context switching, as your stacked commits grow more complex.

To view the conflicts, we can edit the conflicted commit….

In a text editor, we can resolve these conflicts, and the next time we run any jj command, we’ll see that jj has marked the commit as unconflicted:.

Industry observers note that let’s say we made a mistake in that conflict resolution, and we want to undo it. In git, undoing an action, if it’s even possible, is often complicated. In jj, we can always run jj undo:.

More generally, jj maintains a history of all actions in jj op log. We can inspect this log and jj op restore to a point in that history, or jj op revert an individual operation. If the jj undo itself was a mistake, we can jj redo.

The Hint in the output above is a bit of a spoiler for our next topic, the squash workflow.

According to recent reports, editing commits that have descendants can sometimes feel sketchy. If you’re iterating on a large diff that has left your working memory, it would be nice to separate your fresh changes from the existing diff. For example, we might like to inspect the diff that resolves a rebase conflict in isolation.

Let’s follow the instructions from the above output. We first create a newly introduced commit on top of the conflicted commit:.

Now we can resolve the conflicts in main.py in our editor, and rerun jj log:.

We can inspect the diff in @ if we like, and when we’re happy with the conflict resolution, we can squash it into the parent commit:.

The conflict is now resolved, and we can continue our work.

According to recent reports, one of the powerful qualities of jj is that it makes diffs malleable like clay. With automatic rebase and the confidence inspired by jj undo, we can move, combine, drop, and split diffs with ease.

Industry observers note that let’s try a few operations on our current commit graph. Here’s the starting point.

Sources indicate that let’s use jj rebase to coerce our branching commit graph into a linear history. Let’s say the documentation commit (q) should go between the implementation (k) and the usage (n). We could accomplish this by moving nlrtlrxv (and its empty descendant) on top of qwyusntz:.

Another way to accomplish the same effect would be to use jj rebase -r q --before n. Many jj commands have multiple ways to specify revsets. jj rebase --help documents these well.

Since arguments to jj rebase flags are all revsets, we can write a revset that selects a sequence of commits or commit subgraph, and move it elsewhere in the graph.

If we wanted to insert a commit below k, the most direct way is jj new --before k, but for demonstration purposes, we could alternatively create a new commit on top of r and rebase k:: on top:.

If you enjoy using TUIs, jj arrange provides a commit graph editor similar to git rebase -i for reordering commits.

If we decided documentation should be in the same commit as implementation, we can squash:.

jj will open an editor and give us a chance to write a combined commit message.

According to recent reports, to drop a commit from the graph, we can use jj abandon. Let’s drop the preparation commit:.

To abandon parts of a commit (hunks or changes to whole files), we can use the jj diffedit TUI (see docs).

It has been revealed that the jj split TUI allows us to take a commit and split it into two consecutive commits by selecting which files or hunks should go in the first. Let’s use it to split up implementation and documentation again with jj split -r k:.

The jj-hunk project provides a means to automate commit splitting. If you are so inclined, agents are quite good at using this tool to split up commits into a sequence of smaller changes for easier review.

In a recent development, jj does not have a native concept of a branch, but it does have a primitive called bookmarks that map to Git branches. When we need to manipulate Git branches, we do it by way of bookmarks.

According to recent reports, you can go pretty far using Git without realizing this, but a Git branch is just a pointer to a commit. jj explicitly models bookmarks this way. jj bookmarks are essentially a named label attached to a commit that we can move around as we modify our commit graph, and push to/pull from a remote.

We’ll discuss a few basic workflows around Git branches below, but you can find a more complete guide in the jj docs on Working with GitHub.

Assuming we initialized jj in a git repository that has remotes, we should have some output for jj git remote list.

In a recent development, since jj is branchless, the commits we’ve created locally don’t have a branch name. Luckily, jj doesn’t require us to pick one, and generates one for us. Generated branch names free you from thinking of a unique branch name so you can instead focus on writing a good commit message (usually the more durable descriptor of a change).

To create a generated bookmark for change ID nlrtlrxv and push up a corresponding Git branch, we can run a command like the following:.

Now jj log shows our change with a correspondingly named bookmark push-nlrtlrxvuusk associated:.

Recent findings suggest that we’re free to create a PR from this branch on GitHub now. You can customize the bookmark naming scheme with the git_push_bookmark template config documented here. It’s a common pattern to format branch names like /.

Since jj git push -c creates a branch name that corresponds to a change ID, it seems to encourage one evolving change per PR. I think it’s usually best to lean into these ergonomics, and have one change per PR.

To enhancement a branch, the general process is to either squash commits into a change that is already bookmarked, or create new commits and move the bookmark forward.

If you choose to squash commits into an existing bookmark (recommended to keep one change per PR), the flow is as follows.

Sources indicate that first, create a newly introduced commit on top of our branch. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: stzvpxow f14a0cf7 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature Added 2 files, modified 0 files, removed 0 files.

Industry observers note that then make our edits. $ jj status Working copy changes: M README.md Working copy (@) : stzvpxow 6bdd43dc (no description set) Parent commit (@-): nlrtlrxv b1284f61 push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

Squash them into the bookmark branch. $ jj squash --from @ --into push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: xryuuprx 04d65a03 (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk* | Use the feature.

Industry observers note that we now see push-nlrtlrxvuusk has an asterisk next to it, indicating it has changes that haven’t been pushed to the remote. So let’s push them. $ jj git push -b push-nlrtlrxvuusk Changes to push to origin: bookmark: push-nlrtlrxvuusk [move sideways from b1284f61c417 to aeb869aef99b].

In a recent development, the remote branch now reflects the newly introduced changes. The above output states that we moved the branch sideways from one commit to another commit, which reflects that we did a force-push. jj git push runs the equivalent of a git push --force-with-lease, so if you’re ever unclear about what a push operation would do, you can use the jj git push --dry-run flag. jj protects you against most dangerous force pushes refusing to rewrite a configurable revset of immutable commits. The default immutable revset is sensible, but you can make it more or less conservative by configuring your own immutable heads.

In this flow, we add new commits on top of our bookmark and then move the bookmark to point to our new commit.

Let’s first prepare the fresh commit. $ jj new push-nlrtlrxvuusk Working copy (@) now at: pptrztmx 6e49ff1f (empty) (no description set) Parent commit (@-) : nlrtlrxv aeb869ae push-nlrtlrxvuusk | Use the feature.

According to recent reports, the bookmark does not automatically move to our new commit. This is the biggest difference between bookmarks and Git branches. For now push-nlrtlrxvuusk still points at the commit below:.

In a recent development, there are several ways to move the bookmark to the new commit. The easiest is probably jj bookmark advance, which moves the closest bookmark to the given commit:.

Now we’re ready to push the moved bookmark.

Since jj is branchless, strictly speaking, we don’t “check out” a branch, but we can create a commit on top of a remote branch. First do the equivalent of a git fetch, importing remote bookmarks:.

And create a new empty commit on top of the remote branch:.

Our working copy now contains all the commits on the remote branch. However, if we were to drop back to git, we see that from git’s perspective, we’re in a detached head state, not on any branch.

This is because jj is editing a commit above a bookmark, and does not have an equivalent to git’s “current branch” state.

Syncing with the trunk (e.g. main) is just a specific example of this flow. We would jj git fetch to update our main to the upstream main, and then rebase our commits on top. For example, the following would rebase my-branch on top of a new main:.

Industry observers note that jj commit graph manipulation is easiest when you have a live commit graph on screen. There are different ways you can accomplish this.

Recent findings suggest that jjui is a TUI for jj that allows you to edit the visual graph directly. I have not personally used this, but I know people who like it.

I recommend filtering down this log to a revset that represents your current work. Here’s a starting point:.

You might also consider trying my experimental project jj-stamp, which is a local code review GUI for the squash workflow. Even if you don’t use the squash review workflow, it makes a pretty good diff viewer with a live jj log on the side and a terminal for running jj operations.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest productivity gains from jj comes in its ability to support stacked PR workflows. This merits its own post, so I’ll keep it short.

It has been revealed that large changes are easier to understand when they’re broken up into a series of logical steps. Breaking up a large change into smaller sequential atoms of review makes the whole change easier to understand. Stacked PRs attempt to leverage this fact to optimize merge throughput, while simultaneously removing pipeline stalls in the review process.

Recent findings suggest that let’s say we’re building a newly introduced feature. We can decide we want to split up implementation into three stages:.

jj’s ability to work on stacked changes with automatic rebase is a natural fit for implementing these three stages. Each of the three stages maps to a single commit, each with an associated bookmark/branch/PR:.

Sources indicate that after you implement the first change, you can put up a PR for review and immediately start working on the next change. Your work stream becomes a long queue where you pop off the bottom as PRs are ready to merge and push to the top, with no pipeline stalls.

It’s pretty easy to manually set up small PR stacks with jj and GitHub, but once you get hooked on the technique (making stacks 5–10 PRs deep), you’ll want a tool. jj-pancake is my entry into the ring of stacked PR tools. More on that soon.

#3878. Tech Report: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: 5 ways AI will change how you defend your business in 2027

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1171 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities.
  • Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?
  • The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that at the beginning of the year, few organizations were utilizing large language models (LLMs) and AI agents in their cybersecurity workflows, including for discovering and patching vulnerabilities. According to Google, this is now happening at scale.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

The capabilities of agentic AI are fast outstripping the speed and scale at which traditional security operations centers (SOCs) can operate. Like it or not, AI has an integral role in the new reality — for the defenders and threat actors.

It has been revealed that speed and scale are the main reasons enterprises consider adopting AI in SOCs and for security more broadly, and these factors underpin Google’s latest security forecast for 2027 — Cloud CISO Perspectives. However, without the right precautions, AI security adopters could inadvertently increase their attack surface rather than shrink it.

With this in mind, these are five ways AI will change the security industry over the next year and what CISOs need to consider going into 2027.

Sources indicate that alert fatigue is well-known across SOC teams. Alert after alert needs to be trawled through; many are irrelevant or false positives, tying up skilled staff with the mundane, tedious, time-consuming task of triaging them.

Now that autonomous, AI-driven threats can probe a network, gain entry, and move laterally across it in minutes, chasing threat data and security alerts from multiple systems logged days or weeks ago can’t help a business mitigate them — and certainly not at the speed of the threat.

Industry observers note that according to Google’s forecast, AI will mean the alert queue quietly disappears. Ramya Chitrakar, VP of engineering at Google Cloud Security, believes that “2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.”.

Also: AI is both a cyber weapon and a massive target.

How? CISOs must change the alert model itself. Instead of human defenders triaging alerts at the start of a cybersecurity incident, the alert becomes final output, with autonomous agents handling “data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket,” according to Google.

This means cybersecurity experts can oversee alert handling and verify automated actions, potentially freeing them to focus on other tasks.

According to recent reports, custom agentic AI is often designed — or at least intended — to work autonomously, with human oversight. However, having thousands of individual agents working across multiple environments can create high-value entry points into corporate networks that cyberattackers target.

We need to think of agentic AI as more than a tool: each one needs its own identity, like a human employee, to operate within a zero-trust architecture, retain control, and reduce the risk of compromise.

Also: Your enterprise AI access can be sold for pennies – beware ‘LLM Mixers’.

Industry observers note that however, Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering at Google, thinks this needs to go further and suggests the zero-trust concept shouldn’t stop at the network layer. Instead, Adkins believes it needs to reach the transaction layer.

Recent findings suggest that A paper trail for each agent needs to be established, which is impossible to handle manually, and even within a zero-trust framework, AI agents could be given too much scope. Instead, implement verification for each transaction and for every authorization, and assign each AI agent its own least-privilege set of credentials that can be revoked if there is a security incident or the agent is no longer required.

“When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous,” the report notes.

AI is being used to speed up the development and deployment of new software, and in 2027, security will have to become a continuous system embedded in the software delivery pipeline, according to Google.

Threat actors have carried out software supply chain attacks over the years, one of the most notable being the SolarWinds incident of 2020. Sandra Joyce, VP of Google Threat Intelligence, indicates cybercriminals are now poisoning everything from open-source code to software libraries, which AI coding assistants often pull automatically into codebases.

Also: How AI security failures are endangering your supply chain.

Bug-fix tickets that take days to respond to and security appearing at the end of a software development cycle no longer work. Instead, writing and securing code must happen simultaneously, with the help of agentic AI, so speed doesn’t compromise security.

“It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production,” Google added.

As organizations rush to implement AI into their applications and services to appear “AI-first,” innovative, and modern, security may be ignored or treated as an afterthought.

Sources indicate that as a result, we may face a newly introduced, broader attack surface than we realize, as AI introduces new security issues, including software vulnerabilities, misconfiguration, bypasses, and indirect prompt injection attacks. Now that AI is also in the hands of all cyberattackers — from script kiddies to state-sponsored groups — auditing corporate networks and infrastructure is crucial.

Also: Who’s responsible for catching rogue AI agents? You are.

Penetration testing and red team exercises now need to cover agentic AI. This wasn’t in scope for many red teams only a few years ago, but now that businesses have run with the idea of implementing AI in their workflows, processes, and products, organizations need to identify and fix security challenges introduced by AI before threat actors take advantage of them.

CISOs should task pen testers with auditing before an autonomous workflow hits production, then combine the results with threat intelligence to ensure defenders have the information they need to bolster network defenses and harden classifiers against new and novel attacks.

The final significant trend we are likely to see in 2027 is tackling agent sprawl to create coordinated teams of AI agents that can rapidly handle security tasks at scale.

Single AI agents given general instructions won’t cut it when AI-assisted attackers can compromise endpoint devices, enter networks, move laterally, or start stealing data in a far shorter timeframe than before. Instead, CISOs should replace these “generalist” AI agents with specialized, orchestrated teams of AI agents that can meet the demands of defending against AI-driven attacks by employing specialist tooling and skill sets.

Also: AI agent kill switch urged by Okta-led alliance.

Industry observers note that CISOs also need to ensure that each agent has its own domain training and understanding, memory, and dedicated tools, and can act on its own within set limits, with a central coordinator that knows when to hand a decision to a human. This requires oversight, but in return, organizations will avoid agent sprawl, which the tech giant believes is the next iteration of shadow IT and its associated threats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the firm is now rolling out the public beta for owners looking to try the fresh features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several fresh features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

And speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing owners to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing fresh tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful upgrade, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and owners on the public beta can now try out these newly introduced features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.
